extraction.body: Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ) is trading at about $60,652, down 21.7% for the month. This drop is steeper than the 20.5% decline in June, suggesting November could be Bitcoin’s worst month since June 2022. So, why is Bitcoin dropping so much? Five main reasons explain the steep fall. The first factor is substantial outflows from U.S. spot Bitcoin funds, such as the Grayscale Bitcoin Mini Trust ( NYSEARCA: BTC ). On November 24 alone, these funds saw net outflows of $231.6 million, followed by another $453 million shortly after. In total, investors have pulled around $5.14 billion from these funds over the past 30 days. According to Bitfinex, November is on track to see record outflows of about $4.94 billion, after a year in which funds saw outflows on nearly half of all trading days . The second factor is that the supply of stablecoins—the cash equivalent traders use to buy cryptocurrencies—has fallen. It decreased from $300 billion to $283 billion over the past month, representing a drop of about $17 billion, or 5.6%. This reduction leaves traders with less cash available to make purchases, coinciding with the selling pressure from fund investors. The third reason for the price drop is inflation. In October, the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) inflation rate reached 3.8% year over year, and the Federal Reserve had already raised its rate to a 4% upper bound in September. Higher rates make cash and bonds more attractive because they offer better returns, making non-yielding assets like Bitcoin less appealing. Although bond markets have shown slight relief with the 10-year Treasury yield dropping to 4.91% on November 24, this has not been enough to curb the selling trend. The fourth factor is less aggressive buying from Strategy Inc. ( NASDAQ: MSTR | MSTR Price Prediction ), one of Bitcoin’s largest corporate holders. On November 23, Hedgeye reported that Strategy bought only $30 million worth of Bitcoin. With its biggest buyer slowing down, the market has less support, and a look at who is still selling Bitcoin below $59,000 names the sellers adding to the pressure. The fifth reason for Bitcoin’s decline is the Anthropic IPO, which has shifted attention and investment toward AI stocks. On November 20, spot funds saw an outflow of $669.2 million while Bitcoin closed at its 30-day low of $58,818. Earlier pieces examined whether the Anthropic IPO is driving Bitcoin’s decline and whether it is still draining money from crypto . Bitcoin’s ongoing drop can be attributed to reduced fund inflows, limited stablecoin liquidity, minimal corporate buying, the allure of new AI stock offerings, and persistent inflation driving high interest rates. However, sustained inflows into Bitcoin funds or an increase in stablecoin supply could signal renewed buyer interest. As the Federal Reserve’s next meeting approaches on December 9, investors will be watching closely for a cooling inflation report. Such a report could help Bitcoin hold above November’s low of $55,106, which is about 9.1% below its price. If it falls below this level, talk of Bitcoin dropping below $50,000 may resurface. sources.title: Bitcoin Falls Below $59,000, Heading for Worst Month Since June 2022 - Caspian Post
passages: Bitcoin has declined by more than 20% so far this month, according to Yahoo Finance data, marking its steepest monthly drop since June 2022.
If the trend continues, November could become its eighth-worst month since Yahoo Finance began tracking daily bitcoin prices in September 2014.
Bitcoin (BTC) dropped below $59,000 on Friday, extending its November losses and putting the cryptocurrency on track for its worst monthly performance in more than four years.

The digital asset fell to a low of $57,957 during late-morning trading on Friday before recovering some of its losses to trade at around $58,500 by the afternoon, The Caspian Post reports, citing Yahoo Finance .

extraction.body: Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ) is trading at about $60,652, down 21.7% for the month. This drop is steeper than the 20.5% decline in June, suggesting November could be Bitcoin’s worst month since June 2022. So, why is Bitcoin dropping so much? Five main reasons explain the steep fall. The first factor is substantial outflows from U.S. spot Bitcoin funds, such as the Grayscale Bitcoin Mini Trust ( NYSEARCA: BTC ). On November 24 alone, these funds saw net outflows of $231.6 million, followed by another $453 million shortly after. In total, investors have pulled around $5.14 billion from these funds over the past 30 days. According to Bitfinex, November is on track to see record outflows of about $4.94 billion, after a year in which funds saw outflows on nearly half of all trading days . The second factor is that the supply of stablecoins—the cash equivalent traders use to buy cryptocurrencies—has fallen. It decreased from $300 billion to $283 billion over the past month, representing a drop of about $17 billion, or 5.6%. This reduction leaves traders with less cash available to make purchases, coinciding with the selling pressure from fund investors. The third reason for the price drop is inflation. In October, the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) inflation rate reached 3.8% year over year, and the Federal Reserve had already raised its rate to a 4% upper bound in September. Higher rates make cash and bonds more attractive because they offer better returns, making non-yielding assets like Bitcoin less appealing. Although bond markets have shown slight relief with the 10-year Treasury yield dropping to 4.91% on November 24, this has not been enough to curb the selling trend. The fourth factor is less aggressive buying from Strategy Inc. ( NASDAQ: MSTR | MSTR Price Prediction ), one of Bitcoin’s largest corporate holders. On November 23, Hedgeye reported that Strategy bought only $30 million worth of Bitcoin. With its biggest buyer slowing down, the market has less support, and a look at who is still selling Bitcoin below $59,000 names the sellers adding to the pressure. The fifth reason for Bitcoin’s decline is the Anthropic IPO, which has shifted attention and investment toward AI stocks. On November 20, spot funds saw an outflow of $669.2 million while Bitcoin closed at its 30-day low of $58,818. Earlier pieces examined whether the Anthropic IPO is driving Bitcoin’s decline and whether it is still draining money from crypto . Bitcoin’s ongoing drop can be attributed to reduced fund inflows, limited stablecoin liquidity, minimal corporate buying, the allure of new AI stock offerings, and persistent inflation driving high interest rates. However, sustained inflows into Bitcoin funds or an increase in stablecoin supply could signal renewed buyer interest. As the Federal Reserve’s next meeting approaches on December 9, investors will be watching closely for a cooling inflation report. Such a report could help Bitcoin hold above November’s low of $55,106, which is about 9.1% below its price. If it falls below this level, talk of Bitcoin dropping below $50,000 may resurface. extraction.body: The oil and gas infrastructure company’s private discussions with the agency come as the Trump administration loosens a number of environmental requirements for data centers and the natural gas plants being built to power them. “The administration is trying to relax, if not suspend for all intents and purposes, a range of regulatory requirements for these data centers,” says Joseph Goffman, the former assistant administrator at the EPA’s Office of Air and Radiation. “What this administration is trying to do, either explicitly or de facto, is take layers [of regulatory protections] away.” In response to a list of questions from WIRED, Williams spokesperson Alex Schott said in an emailed statement that the company “is committed to developing energy solutions to enhance America’s position in the global competition for AI, while prioritizing environmental protection—including addressing legislation and regulations to modernize construction and implementation timelines.” Meta declined to comment. In July, the EPA announced new federal guidance for states around participation in the Acid Rain Program, following inquiries from “companies and States.” The decades-old program was designed to reduce harmful emissions of chemicals that cause acid rain. Power plants that fall under the program need to submit a permit application two years before a facility comes online, and then regularly monitor emissions to ensure compliance. That month, the EPA said that it recommends that “islanded” power plants—which are increasingly being adopted by data centers across the country—be exempt from the program. Because the program was designed for facilities that sell electricity to the grid, the EPA said, power plants that exclusively power data centers wouldn’t need to comply. Documents obtained by WIRED from the EPA show that Williams was one of three private companies that asked regulators for guidance on the program. In a February letter sent to the Utah Department of Environmental Quality and obtained by WIRED, Williams director of permitting Steve Hall wrote that the “current regulatory uncertainty” around power plants being built solely to power data centers has created “obstacles … for data center development in the United States.” The EPA confirmed to WIRED that Williams sent the agency this letter. Hall wrote that the company believed its power plants “are not subject to the Acid Rain Permit program requirements, as this program was never intended to apply to sources that do not sell power to the public grid.” Getting federal guidance, he wrote, would “accelerate deployment of critical infrastructure” and “support national goals for digital infrastructure and energy reliability in the global AI race.” The EPA said in its July announcement that the new guidance was in keeping with orders from the White House to encourage data center developers to build their own power, in order to avoid increasing utility rates for consumers. However, data center developers are also increasingly turning to private power because it’s often quicker to build their own infrastructure than wait for a grid connection. These private power plants often create more emissions than many of their on-grid counterparts. Williams, one of the top oil and gas infrastructure companies in the country, has emerged in recent years as a power provider for data centers. As of November, Williams had at least six data-center power plant projects in states across the country. Meta is the client for at least four of those projects: four in Ohio, and one in Utah. Calendar invites provided by EPA show that Hall and other executives were invited to at least two meetings with EPA officials, including at least one with Aaron Szabo, then the chief of the agency’s Air office, earlier this year. In an external meeting request form filed with the agency in April, Williams indicated that its request to discuss projects in Ohio and Utah—sites where it is building power plants for Meta—was “urgent.” The EPA confirmed to WIRED that Williams “requested regulatory guidance for both projects” in Ohio and Utah, and that the meetings “broadly discussed air regulations.” “EPA program offices regularly meet with stakeholders in their areas of jurisdiction,” the agency added. Williams’ materials submitted to regulators did not specifically reference its relationship with Meta. But in its official letter on the rule recommendations, the EPA used an example provided by an unnamed company that is building a planned 500-megawatt power plant of simple-cycle natural gas engines “to exclusively power an adjacent, third-party-owned data center.” Williams’ project in Utah and two of its projects in Ohio to power Meta data centers are around 500 megawatts each. Williams first publicly proposed the exemption to the Acid Rain Program in September 2025 in testimony to the House of Representatives from Mark Gebbia, then the company’s vice president of environmental, permitting, and regulatory affairs. In the testimony, Gebbia made several suggestions as to how EPA should change or clarify the implementation of the Clean Air Act, including exempting behind-the-meter data centers from Acid Rain Program requirements. He noted that the long timelines for the permits are “not feasible given the urgent need to install and operate gas-fired generation for AI data centers.” The Acid Rain Program has long been considered a regulatory success that’s ensured coal plants reduce emissions of sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, pollutants that help create acid rain. The law created a cap-and-trade program for power plants, allowing them to buy and sell credits for emissions to keep national levels of the pollutants low. Natural gas plants emit lower levels of these pollutants than traditional coal-fired power plants. The permit application for Williams’ facility to power Meta’s data center in Utah, for example, shows that it could emit a maximum of around 100 tons of nitrogen oxide and 11 tons of sulfur dioxide each year. Other local and national restrictions may limit how much of these pollutants come from natural gas plants. But Acid Rain Program regulations also created crucial reporting requirements that are now in jeopardy for data-center power plants. In the early 1990s, Congress passed an amendment to the Clean Air Act mandating that power facilities monitor and report various emissions in order to establish the program. Now, exempting data-center power plants from complying with the acid rain regulations may jeopardize how much information regulators eventually get about data center emissions—including CO2 emissions, Goffman says. “If the Trump administration was not deranged, and the greenhouse gas reporting program was operating, I think the EPA would be either interpreting that program’s existing requirements to cover these gas plants, or they would be promulgating new regulations to ensure these new gas plants were reporting their greenhouse gas emissions,” he says. Both Goffman and Carrie Jenks, who directs the Environmental and Energy Law Program at Harvard Law School, agree that the EPA’s guidance on the Acid Rain Program for data centers seems to stick to the letter of the law. The program, they say, was explicitly intended to apply only to power plants that sold power to the grid. (Some environmental groups disagree with Goffman and Jenks: Earthjustice and the NRDC sent a letter to the EPA in September challenging the agency’s interpretation of the law in its July recommendation.) When the program was created in 1990, though, wealthy tech companies weren’t rushing to build hundreds of megawatts of private fossil-fuel power that may not ever be connected to the grid. “No one expected it to be economical to develop a bunch of power plants that wouldn’t sell the product they were creating. The program “was never designed to address behind-the-meter generation,” she says. Some estimates show that there’s more than 110 gigawatts of planned behind-the-meter gas projects in the US, with some facilities—like Amazon’s 7-gigawatt facility in Texas, and SoftBank’s 9.2-gigawatt project in Ohio—on track to be some of the largest natural gas plants in the world. Even if those facilities don’t technically qualify for the Acid Rain Program because they’re not on the grid, lawmakers could move to change requirements to make sure that these massive facilities are covered by the program.

One of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade.

extraction.body: The numbers behind the off-grid gas power boom. One of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade. Some developers aren’t willing to wait and are instead opting to build their own off-grid, or behind-the-meter, gas power plants to fuel the AI boom. xAI’s Memphis campus has famously used dozens of natural gas turbines, some of them without permits, as far back as 2024. At the time, that facility was a rarity, and it faced scrutiny from regulators. It remains the subject of ongoing legal battles . Counterintuitively, it is data centers’ independence from the grid and use of natural gas that will hike energy costs for homes and businesses, write experts from Energy Innovation. Jeffrey Rissman is a senior director at at Energy Innovation, where he works on technologies and policies to eliminate industrial greenhouse gas emissions. Eric Gimon is a senior fellow and consults as a technical expert, research scholar and policy adviser with Energy Innovation. A colossal data center is rising amidst the farmlands of Richland Parish, Louisiana. It will guzzle 2.2 GW of power , about twice as much as the entire city of New Orleans on a peak summer day. Near Cheyenne, Wyoming, an even larger data center looms on the horizon. While its first phase requires only 1.8 GW, it is ultimately designed to scale to 10 GW , as much power as all of New York City draws at its peak. Aside from their ravenous power demand, these behemoths share one crucial trait: They will be fed by on-site power plants burning natural gas, not by the electric grid. Counterintuitively, it is data centers’ independence from the grid — coupled with their use of natural gas — that will hike energy costs for American homes and small businesses. To date, most data centers have been powered by the electric grid, but this is changing fast. Facing pressure from policymakers to supply their own power, as well as multi-year delays getting permission to connect to the grid, data center projects increasingly plan to build their own on-site generation capacity, mostly powered by natural gas . A recent Bloomberg New Energy Finance analysis finds 100 GW of on-site gas-burning capacity are planned to power data centers across America. That’s equivalent to 18% of the total existing capacity of all U.S. natural gas power plants , a staggering amount. Building your own natural gas power plant might appear to protect other energy customers by reducing new demand on the grid, but that’s not the case. Natural gas is a market-traded commodity, meaning data centers that gobble up lots of natural gas will naturally compete with other gas customers, increasing prices. That does more than just worsen home heating costs. Since natural gas supplies 43% of U.S. electricity and gas-fired generators set the price of electricity in most hours, higher natural gas prices also raise electricity costs. In fact, data centers with on-site gas plants could spike American energy bills more than connecting those data centers to the grid. That’s because policymakers and regulators can require utilities to charge grid-connected data centers sufficiently high rates to cover their full costs or even enough to help modernize the grid and lower costs for other ratepayers . However, a data center with its own gas power plant signs a contract with a gas supplier, not with a utility, putting its gas rates outside the jurisdiction of state utility regulators. Data centers can buy gas in bulk and sign long-term contracts (as we’ve seen in Texas , Pennsylvania and New Mexico ) , giving them access to cheap gas, even if this unfairly drives up prices for everyone else. Since the most efficient combined-cycle turbines that burn natural gas for electricity are back-ordered for five to seven years , tech firms are relying on inefficient equipment that requires even more gas and creates more pollution. This is creating conflicts across the country, such as in Southaven, Mississippi, where xAI is being sued for violating the Clean Air Act and operating inefficient, polluting gas turbines without a permit. For tech companies, on-site gas plants might seem like a “hack” to speed up power access for data centers, but they’re only exchanging one dependency for another: As tech firms disconnect from the electric grid, they become hooked on the gas grid, where their immense new demand will run into supply bottlenecks, especially during extreme weather like Winter Storm Fern . Meanwhile, their on-site gas strategy will likely come under political pressure as residents demand solutions to rising energy bills and air pollution. Fortunately, there’s a solution that protects data center operators and the public: clean energy. Policymakers should ensure that data centers not simply bring their own electricity — but bring their own clean electricity. Wind and solar backed by batteries, along with enhanced geothermal systems, can be deployed quickly to provide the firm power data centers crave. These energy sources don’t require fuel, so they don’t increase gas or electricity costs for existing customers. And they are affordable — onshore wind and solar are the cheapest forms of generation in America, and they remain cost-competitive with natural gas even when including the cost of batteries. Some tech firms already recognize this opportunity. Google’s upcoming Minnesota data center will be powered by 1.6 GW of wind and solar with 300 MW of battery storage. And Amazon recently outbid a local utility to purchase 1.2 GW of solar capacity and an equal amount of battery storage to supply its Oregon data centers. While clean energy is already an affordable and reliable solution, policy can help make it standard for data centers. State policymakers can use siting and zoning requirements, air quality regulations, or new legislation to require that data centers build enough pollution-free capacity to supply their electricity needs, protecting communities and electric ratepayers. This must be accompanied by permitting, siting and interconnection support that allows clean energy to quickly meet new demand. For instance, states can adopt “permit-by-rule” to automatically permit renewable energy projects that comply with standardized regulations. States should also pre-authorize zones where renewables and transmission can connect without extensive permits or impact assessments such as Texas’ Competitive Renewable Energy Zones , Nevada’s Solar Energy Zones , and Arizona’s Renewable Energy Incentive Districts . Simultaneously, they should set standards that harmonize local permitting requirements and prevent localities from enforcing onerous rules intended to block renewables. Smart examples include Michigan’s HB 5120 and Illinois’s HB 4412 , both enacted in 2023. Public support for data center development is at an all-time low. Most U.S. voters now oppose data centers out of concern for their impacts on home energy costs, the environment and the quality of life of nearby residents, which can be harmed by constant noise and soot from gas turbines. A “bring your own clean energy” mandate can help address all three concerns, ensuring the data centers powering the AI revolution don’t come at the expense of Americans’ wallets, health and well-being. Part of the document states companies must buy the massive amount of electricity they require, add more power to the grid or supply it on-site. “You're going to be building your own data centers, and you're going to be building your own electric plants,” said President Donald Trump. “You're essentially becoming a utility.” The pledge is one of many ways officials are responding to public pushback against hyperscale data centers. State regulators are currently reviewing large-load tariffs from utilities intended to prevent households from shouldering grid connection costs for companies like Google and Meta. The legislature also passed Senate Bill 480 last year, allowing data centers to build power plants behind the meter, bypassing utilities. Rep. Brad Boles, R-Marlow, co-authored the legislation. “What we realized is in Oklahoma, our state law is kind of vague; it doesn't really say that companies can provide their own power generation,” Boles, who is running for a seat on the Corporation Commission, said. “It doesn't say they can't either, but it doesn't say that they can.” “ So we wanted to provide clarity that if a large load comes to Oklahoma and they want to provide their own power generation, that they would have the ability to do that,” he said. The bill was expected to generate billions of dollars in private investment and alleviate pressure from the electric grid. Growing demand, supercharged by large-load consumers like data centers, is expected to outpace supply within the Southwest Power Pool’s territory. The organization operates the electric grid in Oklahoma and 16 other states. But so far, most data centers with plans in Oklahoma are opting to plug into the grid. Experts say the state’s grid system is likely more reliable than depending on behind-the-meter generation. Building a power plant is costly and can take years to complete. “ I don't readily, actually, believe that any data center company wants to also be in the power business,” said Joshua Rhodes, a research scientist at the University of Texas at Austin. Still, some AI companies are investing in behind-the-meter natural gas plants in states like neighboring Texas to accelerate the pace of buildout. Those plants are expected to emit significant amounts of pollution, an analysis from the Texas Tribune and Floodlight shows. Data centers typically have backup generators on site, should they temporarily lose connection. Some companies are adding power to the grid with new energy projects. Google and Oklahoma Gas & Electric announced a deal in the spring to power the tech company’s three data centers in Muskogee and Stillwater. Google is building two solar farms to add energy generation. Christi Woodworth, OG&E's chief communications officer, said companies are eyeing the state’s relatively low electricity costs and reliability. “They've got to make a decision about if they want to build or bring their own generation,” she said. “That effectively puts them on an island, right? They take on all of that risk themselves, and they have to decide if that's something that they want to do.” “The folks we're talking with are very interested in connecting to the grid.” The company is in “a handful” of other discussions with large-load projects, Woodworth said, but no plans are public yet. A news release says the company specializes in aerospace, energy and advanced manufacturing. Large proposed data centers, including the Luther Horizon Technology Park, Project Mustang in Claremore, IREN’s Kiowa Data Center and more, plan to work with local utilities. The Kiowa facility is the state’s largest proposed data center, according to energy analytics firm Cleanview . In an email, Jason Date, associate director of development, said the company plans to secure its power through Public Service Company of Oklahoma. "Like the vast majority of homes and businesses, IREN's facilities use grid power because it is the most efficient and reliable way to source electricity,” he said. A delay in critical infrastructure delivery is also an obstacle for data center developers. Getting a natural gas plant, the typical energy source for behind-the-meter data center projects, can currently take years . “If you're not in line right now, you're probably not getting one until the 2030s,” Rhodes said. Some companies instead are turning to used products to avoid the mile-long backlog. “ I've heard of companies looking to buy used cruise ship engines,” Rhodes said. “I heard one the other day of someone trying to string together a bunch of used helicopter engines.” Oklahoma’s behind-the-meter law requires developers to have natural gas as part of their plant. Other sources, including solar and wind, could be used in conjunction. When asked about the natural gas requirement, Boles said it was included to support the oil and gas industry. “We felt like, as Oklahomans, it's important to ensure that natural gas has a seat at the table,” he said. According to an analysis from Cleanview, Oklahoma has fewer than 30 data centers planned for the state as of early August. Texas has hundreds in its queue, Rhodes said, meaning more developers are racing to supply power. Should tech companies continue showing interest in Oklahoma, it’s possible more behind-the-meter projects could be announced. Boles said he expects more interest in the future. “Like anything, it takes time,” Boles said. “If you're to build a facility with behind-the-meter, it may take three to five years to get the power infrastructure built.” “I think we're not going to really know for sure how many companies are utilizing this until a few years down the road.”

coreStoryFacts.text: Now, exempting data-center power plants from complying with the acid rain regulations may jeopardize how much information regulators eventually get about data center emissions—including CO2 emissions, Goffman says.

But in its official letter on the rule recommendations, the EPA used an example provided by an unnamed company that is building a planned 500-megawatt power plant of simple-cycle natural gas engines “to exclusively power an adjacent, third-party-owned data center.” Williams’ project in Utah and two of its projects in Ohio to power Meta data centers are around 500 megawatts each.

In the testimony, Gebbia made several suggestions as to how EPA should change or clarify the implementation of the Clean Air Act, including exempting behind-the-meter data centers from Acid Rain Program requirements.
However, data center developers are also increasingly turning to private power because it’s often quicker to build their own infrastructure than wait for a grid connection.

The program, they say, was explicitly intended to apply only to power plants that sold power to the grid. (Some environmental groups disagree with Goffman and Jenks: Earthjustice and the NRDC sent a letter to the EPA in September challenging the agency’s interpretation of the law in its July recommendation.) When the program was created in 1990, though, wealthy tech companies weren’t rushing to build hundreds of megawatts of private fossil-fuel power that may not ever be connected to the grid.
These private power plants often create more emissions than many of their on-grid counterparts.
Williams’ materials submitted to regulators did not specifically reference its relationship with Meta.
Natural gas plants emit lower levels of these pollutants than traditional coal-fired power plants.
BloombergNEF is also tracking on-site natural gas plants at data centers, finding 181 gigawatts’ worth of announced projects globally, with 90% of that capacity designated for the US.
One of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade.
Some developers aren’t willing to wait and are instead opting to build their own off-grid, or behind-the-meter, gas power plants to fuel the AI boom.

“This shift in the data center developers’ power strategies towards off-grid gas raises some important questions about how data centers will be powered going forward,” says Brendan Pierpont, director of electricity at the think tank Energy Innovation.
“These data centers want a lot of power, and they want it fast, and the grid is not well equipped to provide that,” Fripp says.
That means these off-grid plants will likely produce more greenhouse-gas emissions than even other natural gas resources.
In fact, data centers with on-site gas plants could spike American energy bills more than connecting those data centers to the grid.
However, a data center with its own gas power plant signs a contract with a gas supplier, not with a utility, putting its gas rates outside the jurisdiction of state utility regulators.
Michigan is among the states weighing reforms to rate case planning and utility profits.
Experts and stakeholders told Utility Dive what works — and what doesn’t.
That’s equivalent to 18% of the total existing capacity of all U.S. natural gas power plants , a staggering amount.
Google’s upcoming Minnesota data center will be powered by 1.6 GW of wind and solar with 300 MW of battery storage.

extraction.body: The oil and gas infrastructure company’s private discussions with the agency come as the Trump administration loosens a number of environmental requirements for data centers and the natural gas plants being built to power them. “The administration is trying to relax, if not suspend for all intents and purposes, a range of regulatory requirements for these data centers,” says Joseph Goffman, the former assistant administrator at the EPA’s Office of Air and Radiation. “What this administration is trying to do, either explicitly or de facto, is take layers [of regulatory protections] away.” In response to a list of questions from WIRED, Williams spokesperson Alex Schott said in an emailed statement that the company “is committed to developing energy solutions to enhance America’s position in the global competition for AI, while prioritizing environmental protection—including addressing legislation and regulations to modernize construction and implementation timelines.” Meta declined to comment. In July, the EPA announced new federal guidance for states around participation in the Acid Rain Program, following inquiries from “companies and States.” The decades-old program was designed to reduce harmful emissions of chemicals that cause acid rain. Power plants that fall under the program need to submit a permit application two years before a facility comes online, and then regularly monitor emissions to ensure compliance. That month, the EPA said that it recommends that “islanded” power plants—which are increasingly being adopted by data centers across the country—be exempt from the program. Because the program was designed for facilities that sell electricity to the grid, the EPA said, power plants that exclusively power data centers wouldn’t need to comply. Documents obtained by WIRED from the EPA show that Williams was one of three private companies that asked regulators for guidance on the program. In a February letter sent to the Utah Department of Environmental Quality and obtained by WIRED, Williams director of permitting Steve Hall wrote that the “current regulatory uncertainty” around power plants being built solely to power data centers has created “obstacles … for data center development in the United States.” The EPA confirmed to WIRED that Williams sent the agency this letter. Hall wrote that the company believed its power plants “are not subject to the Acid Rain Permit program requirements, as this program was never intended to apply to sources that do not sell power to the public grid.” Getting federal guidance, he wrote, would “accelerate deployment of critical infrastructure” and “support national goals for digital infrastructure and energy reliability in the global AI race.” The EPA said in its July announcement that the new guidance was in keeping with orders from the White House to encourage data center developers to build their own power, in order to avoid increasing utility rates for consumers. However, data center developers are also increasingly turning to private power because it’s often quicker to build their own infrastructure than wait for a grid connection. These private power plants often create more emissions than many of their on-grid counterparts. Williams, one of the top oil and gas infrastructure companies in the country, has emerged in recent years as a power provider for data centers. As of November, Williams had at least six data-center power plant projects in states across the country. Meta is the client for at least four of those projects: four in Ohio, and one in Utah. Calendar invites provided by EPA show that Hall and other executives were invited to at least two meetings with EPA officials, including at least one with Aaron Szabo, then the chief of the agency’s Air office, earlier this year. In an external meeting request form filed with the agency in April, Williams indicated that its request to discuss projects in Ohio and Utah—sites where it is building power plants for Meta—was “urgent.” The EPA confirmed to WIRED that Williams “requested regulatory guidance for both projects” in Ohio and Utah, and that the meetings “broadly discussed air regulations.” “EPA program offices regularly meet with stakeholders in their areas of jurisdiction,” the agency added. Williams’ materials submitted to regulators did not specifically reference its relationship with Meta. But in its official letter on the rule recommendations, the EPA used an example provided by an unnamed company that is building a planned 500-megawatt power plant of simple-cycle natural gas engines “to exclusively power an adjacent, third-party-owned data center.” Williams’ project in Utah and two of its projects in Ohio to power Meta data centers are around 500 megawatts each. Williams first publicly proposed the exemption to the Acid Rain Program in September 2025 in testimony to the House of Representatives from Mark Gebbia, then the company’s vice president of environmental, permitting, and regulatory affairs. In the testimony, Gebbia made several suggestions as to how EPA should change or clarify the implementation of the Clean Air Act, including exempting behind-the-meter data centers from Acid Rain Program requirements. He noted that the long timelines for the permits are “not feasible given the urgent need to install and operate gas-fired generation for AI data centers.” The Acid Rain Program has long been considered a regulatory success that’s ensured coal plants reduce emissions of sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, pollutants that help create acid rain. The law created a cap-and-trade program for power plants, allowing them to buy and sell credits for emissions to keep national levels of the pollutants low. Natural gas plants emit lower levels of these pollutants than traditional coal-fired power plants. The permit application for Williams’ facility to power Meta’s data center in Utah, for example, shows that it could emit a maximum of around 100 tons of nitrogen oxide and 11 tons of sulfur dioxide each year. Other local and national restrictions may limit how much of these pollutants come from natural gas plants. But Acid Rain Program regulations also created crucial reporting requirements that are now in jeopardy for data-center power plants. In the early 1990s, Congress passed an amendment to the Clean Air Act mandating that power facilities monitor and report various emissions in order to establish the program. Now, exempting data-center power plants from complying with the acid rain regulations may jeopardize how much information regulators eventually get about data center emissions—including CO2 emissions, Goffman says. “If the Trump administration was not deranged, and the greenhouse gas reporting program was operating, I think the EPA would be either interpreting that program’s existing requirements to cover these gas plants, or they would be promulgating new regulations to ensure these new gas plants were reporting their greenhouse gas emissions,” he says. Both Goffman and Carrie Jenks, who directs the Environmental and Energy Law Program at Harvard Law School, agree that the EPA’s guidance on the Acid Rain Program for data centers seems to stick to the letter of the law. The program, they say, was explicitly intended to apply only to power plants that sold power to the grid. (Some environmental groups disagree with Goffman and Jenks: Earthjustice and the NRDC sent a letter to the EPA in September challenging the agency’s interpretation of the law in its July recommendation.) When the program was created in 1990, though, wealthy tech companies weren’t rushing to build hundreds of megawatts of private fossil-fuel power that may not ever be connected to the grid. “No one expected it to be economical to develop a bunch of power plants that wouldn’t sell the product they were creating. The program “was never designed to address behind-the-meter generation,” she says. Some estimates show that there’s more than 110 gigawatts of planned behind-the-meter gas projects in the US, with some facilities—like Amazon’s 7-gigawatt facility in Texas, and SoftBank’s 9.2-gigawatt project in Ohio—on track to be some of the largest natural gas plants in the world. Even if those facilities don’t technically qualify for the Acid Rain Program because they’re not on the grid, lawmakers could move to change requirements to make sure that these massive facilities are covered by the program.

extraction.body: The numbers behind the off-grid gas power boom. One of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade. Some developers aren’t willing to wait and are instead opting to build their own off-grid, or behind-the-meter, gas power plants to fuel the AI boom. xAI’s Memphis campus has famously used dozens of natural gas turbines, some of them without permits, as far back as 2024. At the time, that facility was a rarity, and it faced scrutiny from regulators. It remains the subject of ongoing legal battles . But the strategy of going off-grid for power has since become a lot more common. As of October 2026, data center developers have announced plans for more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants at facilities in the US, according to data from Cleanview, a market intelligence company. The facilities have a combined planned capacity of over 115 gigawatts, more than double the peak power demand of California. The vast majority of these announcements have come since the beginning of 2025. It’s possible that not all these facilities will be built; only a small fraction are under construction or operating today. But there’s a growing trend of large data centers looking to build their own power supply, and this could shape the grid—and its climate impacts—for decades to come. Building your own power plant is generally more expensive than just hooking up to the grid, but the AI rush has made developers willing to pay a significant premium to get online faster. “The biggest motivator for on-site power right now from data centers is speed,” says Musfika Mishi, an associate at BloombergNEF, an energy consultancy. When developers want to build a new industrial facility—like a data center—that requires a lot of electricity, they need to request a grid connection from a local utility or regional grid operator. That request kicks off a yearslong process in which grid planners study the existing grid to understand what would need to be built to safely deliver power to the facility without compromising reliability. Upgrades might be required, like building new transmission lines or larger transformers, and the developer might be on the hook to help pay for them. Rather than waiting for that process to play out, developers can opt to instead build their own power plants. These facilities are referred to as “behind the meter” because they sit on the customer’s side of a utility meter—supplying the building directly, rather than relying on a utility via a grid hookup. “This shift in the data center developers’ power strategies towards off-grid gas raises some important questions about how data centers will be powered going forward,” says Brendan Pierpont, director of electricity at the think tank Energy Innovation. Behind-the-meter doesn’t always mean being totally disconnected from the grid, however. Some facilities may build such plants as a temporary measure, eventually connecting to the grid and tapping their own power plants only as backup. “It’s really just a very expensive way to bridge that maybe five-to-seven-year timeline gap until these data centers can get a grid connection,” Pierpont says. Even if gas plants are pitched as a near-term solution, building new fossil fuel infrastructure could lead to longer-term effects, since an operator might choose to continue running plants once they’ve spent money building them. “Even though data centers say that it’s a grid-bridging solution, the probability that it is going to be in use much longer is a real risk, and that leads to fossil fuel lock-in,” Mishi says. The on-site gas rush could have major implications for greenhouse-gas emissions. Today, the US grid is still reliant on fossil fuels, but nuclear and renewables together make up about 40% of electricity generation. That means making a grid connection is generally a lower-emissions option than relying entirely on an on-site gas plant. (That’s not the case everywhere—India, for example, is expecting to see a data center boom in the next decade, and its grid is largely served by emissions-intensive coal-fired power plants today.) Utilities are already planning to build more natural gas power plants on the grid to meet rising electricity demand. Equipment manufacturers are struggling to keep up with the surge, and it’s pushing developers of behind-the-meter plants toward less-efficient alternatives. Today, large natural gas plants generally use combined-cycle turbines. These capture heat to generate additional electricity, making them more efficient than single-cycle turbines, which are generally cheaper to build. Very few of the planned behind-the-meter facilities, however, will use combined-cycle turbines, Mishi says. That means these off-grid plants will likely produce more greenhouse-gas emissions than even other natural gas resources. BloombergNEF is also tracking on-site natural gas plants at data centers, finding 181 gigawatts’ worth of announced projects globally, with 90% of that capacity designated for the US. If all planned behind-the-meter gas plants for data centers in the US go ahead, they could emit 345 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent each year by 2035, according to a BloombergNEF report . That’s 152 million metric tons more than if those data centers pulled power from the US grid—a difference greater than the total annual emissions of the Netherlands. And while it might seem logical that data centers bringing their own power could ease communities’ energy bills, those facilities going off-grid doesn’t protect prices for everyone else, says Matthias Fripp, director of global policy research at Energy Innovation. More demand for natural gas could push its price higher, he explains, which could in turn raise rates for the roughly 60% of American households that use natural gas for heating and cooking. That effect may also trickle into electricity prices. There’s still a lot of uncertainty about how much of this gas rush will come to fruition, so this future isn’t set in stone. Today, just 4.9 gigawatts of behind-the-meter gas projects tied to data centers are operating, and 15.8 gigawatts are under construction, according to Cleanview’s data. Creative solutions could also help limit the climate burden of the on-site gas buildout, BloombergNEF’s Mishi says. Building gas alongside on-site renewables or energy storage could help limit how often a gas plant needs to fire up, she says, though the economics of building multiple energy sources can be tricky. While the grid is struggling to keep up with demand, building more renewables could help, Fripp adds. passages: The numbers behind the off-grid gas power boom.

One of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade. Some developers aren’t willing to wait and are instead opting to build their own off-grid, or behind-the-meter, gas power plants to fuel the AI boom.

xAI’s Memphis campus has famously used dozens of natural gas turbines, some of them without permits, as far back as 2024. At the time, that facility was a rarity, and it faced scrutiny from regulators. It remains the subject of ongoing legal battles . But the strategy of going off-grid for power has since become a lot more common.

As of October 2026, data center developers have announced plans for more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants at facilities in the US, according to data from Cleanview, a market intelligence company. The facilities have a combined planned capacity of over 115 gigawatts, more than double the peak power demand of California. The vast majority of these announcements have come since the beginning of 2025.

It’s possible that not all these facilities will be built; only a small fraction are under construction or operating today. But there’s a growing trend of large data centers looking to build their own power supply, and this could shape the grid—and its climate impacts—for decades to come.

Building your own power plant is generally more expensive than just hooking up to the grid, but the AI rush has made developers willing to pay a significant premium to get online faster. “The biggest motivator for on-site power right now from data centers is speed,” says Musfika Mishi, an associate at BloombergNEF, an energy consultancy.

When developers want to build a new industrial facility—like a data center—that requires a lot of electricity, they need to request a grid connection from a local utility or regional grid operator. That request kicks off a yearslong process in which grid planners study the existing grid to understand what would need to be built to safely deliver power to the facility without compromising reliability. Upgrades might be required, like building new transmission lines or larger transformers, and the developer might be on the hook to help pay for them.

Rather than waiting for that process to play out, developers can opt to instead build their own power plants. These facilities are referred to as “behind the meter” because they sit on the customer’s side of a utility meter—supplying the building directly, rather than relying on a utility via a grid hookup.

“This shift in the data center developers’ power strategies towards off-grid gas raises some important questions about how data centers will be powered going forward,” says Brendan Pierpont, director of electricity at the think tank Energy Innovation.

Behind-the-meter doesn’t always mean being totally disconnected from the grid, however. Some facilities may build such plants as a temporary measure, eventually connecting to the grid and tapping their own power plants only as backup. “It’s really just a very expensive way to bridge that maybe five-to-seven-year timeline gap until these data centers can get a grid connection,” Pierpont says.

Even if gas plants are pitched as a near-term solution, building new fossil fuel infrastructure could lead to longer-term effects, since an operator might choose to continue running plants once they’ve spent money building them. “Even though data centers say that it’s a grid-bridging solution, the probability that it is going to be in use much longer is a real risk, and that leads to fossil fuel lock-in,” Mishi says.

The on-site gas rush could have major implications for greenhouse-gas emissions. Today, the US grid is still reliant on fossil fuels, but nuclear and renewables together make up about 40% of electricity generation. That means making a grid connection is generally a lower-emissions option than relying entirely on an on-site gas plant. (That’s not the case everywhere—India, for example, is expecting to see a data center boom in the next decade, and its grid is largely served by emissions-intensive coal-fired power plants today.)

Utilities are already planning to build more natural gas power plants on the grid to meet rising electricity demand. Equipment manufacturers are struggling to keep up with the surge, and it’s pushing developers of behind-the-meter plants toward less-efficient alternatives.

Today, large natural gas plants generally use combined-cycle turbines. These capture heat to generate additional electricity, making them more efficient than single-cycle turbines, which are generally cheaper to build. Very few of the planned behind-the-meter facilities, however, will use combined-cycle turbines, Mishi says. That means these off-grid plants will likely produce more greenhouse-gas emissions than even other natural gas resources.

BloombergNEF is also tracking on-site natural gas plants at data centers, finding 181 gigawatts’ worth of announced projects globally, with 90% of that capacity designated for the US. If all planned behind-the-meter gas plants for data centers in the US go ahead, they could emit 345 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent each year by 2035, according to a BloombergNEF report . That’s 152 million metric tons more than if those data centers pulled power from the US grid—a difference greater than the total annual emissions of the Netherlands.

And while it might seem logical that data centers bringing their own power could ease communities’ energy bills, those facilities going off-grid doesn’t protect prices for everyone else, says Matthias Fripp, director of global policy research at Energy Innovation. More demand for natural gas could push its price higher, he explains, which could in turn raise rates for the roughly 60% of American households that use natural gas for heating and cooking. That effect may also trickle into electricity prices.

There’s still a lot of uncertainty about how much of this gas rush will come to fruition, so this future isn’t set in stone. Today, just 4.9 gigawatts of behind-the-meter gas projects tied to data centers are operating, and 15.8 gigawatts are under construction, according to Cleanview’s data.

Creative solutions could also help limit the climate burden of the on-site gas buildout, BloombergNEF’s Mishi says. Building gas alongside on-site renewables or energy storage could help limit how often a gas plant needs to fire up, she says, though the economics of building multiple energy sources can be tricky.

While the grid is struggling to keep up with demand, building more renewables could help, Fripp adds. In a recent study , his team found that building renewables and energy storage to meet rising electricity demand could be reliable and cheaper than relying on fossil fuels.

“These data centers want a lot of power, and they want it fast, and the grid is not well equipped to provide that,” Fripp says. “There are potentially good solutions and bad solutions … Rushing off the grid and putting in your own behind-the-meter gas is probably a bad way, because it’s still going to raise other people’s bills, and it’s not great for the environment.”

Counterintuitively, it is data centers’ independence from the grid and use of natural gas that will hike energy costs for homes and businesses, write experts from Energy Innovation. Jeffrey Rissman is a senior director at at Energy Innovation, where he works on technologies and policies to eliminate industrial greenhouse gas emissions. Eric Gimon is a senior fellow and consults as a technical expert, research scholar and policy adviser with Energy Innovation. A colossal data center is rising amidst the farmlands of Richland Parish, Louisiana. It will guzzle 2.2 GW of power , about twice as much as the entire city of New Orleans on a peak summer day. Near Cheyenne, Wyoming, an even larger data center looms on the horizon. While its first phase requires only 1.8 GW, it is ultimately designed to scale to 10 GW , as much power as all of New York City draws at its peak. Aside from their ravenous power demand, these behemoths share one crucial trait: They will be fed by on-site power plants burning natural gas, not by the electric grid. Counterintuitively, it is data centers’ independence from the grid — coupled with their use of natural gas — that will hike energy costs for American homes and small businesses. To date, most data centers have been powered by the electric grid, but this is changing fast. Facing pressure from policymakers to supply their own power, as well as multi-year delays getting permission to connect to the grid, data center projects increasingly plan to build their own on-site generation capacity, mostly powered by natural gas . A recent Bloomberg New Energy Finance analysis finds 100 GW of on-site gas-burning capacity are planned to power data centers across America. That’s equivalent to 18% of the total existing capacity of all U.S. natural gas power plants , a staggering amount. Building your own natural gas power plant might appear to protect other energy customers by reducing new demand on the grid, but that’s not the case. Natural gas is a market-traded commodity, meaning data centers that gobble up lots of natural gas will naturally compete with other gas customers, increasing prices. That does more than just worsen home heating costs. Since natural gas supplies 43% of U.S. electricity and gas-fired generators set the price of electricity in most hours, higher natural gas prices also raise electricity costs. In fact, data centers with on-site gas plants could spike American energy bills more than connecting those data centers to the grid. That’s because policymakers and regulators can require utilities to charge grid-connected data centers sufficiently high rates to cover their full costs or even enough to help modernize the grid and lower costs for other ratepayers . However, a data center with its own gas power plant signs a contract with a gas supplier, not with a utility, putting its gas rates outside the jurisdiction of state utility regulators. Data centers can buy gas in bulk and sign long-term contracts (as we’ve seen in Texas , Pennsylvania and New Mexico ) , giving them access to cheap gas, even if this unfairly drives up prices for everyone else. Since the most efficient combined-cycle turbines that burn natural gas for electricity are back-ordered for five to seven years , tech firms are relying on inefficient equipment that requires even more gas and creates more pollution. This is creating conflicts across the country, such as in Southaven, Mississippi, where xAI is being sued for violating the Clean Air Act and operating inefficient, polluting gas turbines without a permit. For tech companies, on-site gas plants might seem like a “hack” to speed up power access for data centers, but they’re only exchanging one dependency for another: As tech firms disconnect from the electric grid, they become hooked on the gas grid, where their immense new demand will run into supply bottlenecks, especially during extreme weather like Winter Storm Fern . Meanwhile, their on-site gas strategy will likely come under political pressure as residents demand solutions to rising energy bills and air pollution. Fortunately, there’s a solution that protects data center operators and the public: clean energy. Policymakers should ensure that data centers not simply bring their own electricity — but bring their own clean electricity. Wind and solar backed by batteries, along with enhanced geothermal systems, can be deployed quickly to provide the firm power data centers crave. These energy sources don’t require fuel, so they don’t increase gas or electricity costs for existing customers. And they are affordable — onshore wind and solar are the cheapest forms of generation in America, and they remain cost-competitive with natural gas even when including the cost of batteries. Some tech firms already recognize this opportunity. Google’s upcoming Minnesota data center will be powered by 1.6 GW of wind and solar with 300 MW of battery storage. And Amazon recently outbid a local utility to purchase 1.2 GW of solar capacity and an equal amount of battery storage to supply its Oregon data centers. While clean energy is already an affordable and reliable solution, policy can help make it standard for data centers. State policymakers can use siting and zoning requirements, air quality regulations, or new legislation to require that data centers build enough pollution-free capacity to supply their electricity needs, protecting communities and electric ratepayers. This must be accompanied by permitting, siting and interconnection support that allows clean energy to quickly meet new demand. For instance, states can adopt “permit-by-rule” to automatically permit renewable energy projects that comply with standardized regulations. States should also pre-authorize zones where renewables and transmission can connect without extensive permits or impact assessments such as Texas’ Competitive Renewable Energy Zones , Nevada’s Solar Energy Zones , and Arizona’s Renewable Energy Incentive Districts . Simultaneously, they should set standards that harmonize local permitting requirements and prevent localities from enforcing onerous rules intended to block renewables. Smart examples include Michigan’s HB 5120 and Illinois’s HB 4412 , both enacted in 2023. Public support for data center development is at an all-time low. Most U.S. voters now oppose data centers out of concern for their impacts on home energy costs, the environment and the quality of life of nearby residents, which can be harmed by constant noise and soot from gas turbines. A “bring your own clean energy” mandate can help address all three concerns, ensuring the data centers powering the AI revolution don’t come at the expense of Americans’ wallets, health and well-being. extraction.body: Last month, Gov. Kevin Stitt and some Oklahoma electric utilities signed a federal pledge to protect household ratepayers. The Ratepayer Protection Pledge directs data center developers to pay their own way and invest in surrounding communities. Part of the document states companies must buy the massive amount of electricity they require, add more power to the grid or supply it on-site. “You're going to be building your own data centers, and you're going to be building your own electric plants,” said President Donald Trump. “You're essentially becoming a utility.” The pledge is one of many ways officials are responding to public pushback against hyperscale data centers. Oklahoma has its own version of a ratepayer protection pledge , a law requiring electricity suppliers to create separate terms and conditions for large-scale energy consumers like data centers and increase transparency. State regulators are currently reviewing large-load tariffs from utilities intended to prevent households from shouldering grid connection costs for companies like Google and Meta. The legislature also passed Senate Bill 480 last year, allowing data centers to build power plants behind the meter, bypassing utilities. Rep. Brad Boles, R-Marlow, co-authored the legislation. “What we realized is in Oklahoma, our state law is kind of vague; it doesn't really say that companies can provide their own power generation,” Boles, who is running for a seat on the Corporation Commission, said. “It doesn't say they can't either, but it doesn't say that they can.” “ So we wanted to provide clarity that if a large load comes to Oklahoma and they want to provide their own power generation, that they would have the ability to do that,” he said. The bill was expected to generate billions of dollars in private investment and alleviate pressure from the electric grid. Growing demand, supercharged by large-load consumers like data centers, is expected to outpace supply within the Southwest Power Pool’s territory. The organization operates the electric grid in Oklahoma and 16 other states. But so far, most data centers with plans in Oklahoma are opting to plug into the grid. Experts say the state’s grid system is likely more reliable than depending on behind-the-meter generation. Building a power plant is costly and can take years to complete. “ I don't readily, actually, believe that any data center company wants to also be in the power business,” said Joshua Rhodes, a research scientist at the University of Texas at Austin. Still, some AI companies are investing in behind-the-meter natural gas plants in states like neighboring Texas to accelerate the pace of buildout. Those plants are expected to emit significant amounts of pollution, an analysis from the Texas Tribune and Floodlight shows. Data centers typically have backup generators on site, should they temporarily lose connection. Some companies are adding power to the grid with new energy projects. Google and Oklahoma Gas & Electric announced a deal in the spring to power the tech company’s three data centers in Muskogee and Stillwater. Google is building two solar farms to add energy generation. Christi Woodworth, OG&E's chief communications officer, said companies are eyeing the state’s relatively low electricity costs and reliability. “They've got to make a decision about if they want to build or bring their own generation,” she said. “That effectively puts them on an island, right? They take on all of that risk themselves, and they have to decide if that's something that they want to do.” “The folks we're talking with are very interested in connecting to the grid.” The company is in “a handful” of other discussions with large-load projects, Woodworth said, but no plans are public yet. sources.title: US approves SpaceX plan to send a million data satellites to space - BBC
passages: US regulators have given SpaceX the go-ahead to launch a million satellites into Earth's orbit to help build data centres in space - the first approval of its kind.
Under the FCC licence, deployment of the satellites must begin no later than November 2033.
SpaceX will be required to have deployed 10% by November 2035, rising to 50% by November 2038.
SpaceX is an aerospace company that builds rockets and spacecraft, as well as running satellite services

SpaceX believes the "orbital data centres" are the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) computing power that is beyond "terrestrial capabilities".

Like SpaceX's current Starlink network, which provides high-speed internet via more than 10,000 satellites, Starmind's satellites will operate in low-Earth orbit at altitudes ranging between 500-2,000km (310-1,242 miles).
The company, which is owned by Elon Musk, wants to use sunlight to power satellites that will process data for AI and send the results back to Earth.

extraction.body: SpaceX is an aerospace company that builds rockets and spacecraft, as well as running satellite services US regulators have given SpaceX the go-ahead to launch a million satellites into Earth's orbit to help build data centres in space - the first approval of its kind. The company, which is owned by Elon Musk, wants to use sunlight to power satellites that will process data for AI and send the results back to Earth. The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said on Wednesday that the project, known as Starmind, would "support America's booming super intelligence economy". However, rival firm Amazon has criticised it as a "lofty ambition rather than a real plan", while astronomers in the US said the move would "significantly undermine" the public's ability to study and observe the night sky. There is increasing opposition to data centres on earth, including in the US where experts say they were a factor in the Republicans big losses in the midterm elections. SpaceX believes the "orbital data centres" are the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) computing power that is beyond "terrestrial capabilities". FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement that the project "opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth". "This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home," Carr said. Responding to the announcement, Musk wrote on X: "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world." Why Canada is embracing AI data centres while the US pushes back Under the FCC licence, deployment of the satellites must begin no later than November 2033. SpaceX will be required to have deployed 10% by November 2035, rising to 50% by November 2038. The company has already said it wants to launch its first Starmind satellite next year. It is unclear whether a million satellites will indeed be launched or whether SpaceX has sought approval for a higher number than it will use. Like SpaceX's current Starlink network, which provides high-speed internet via more than 10,000 satellites, Starmind's satellites will operate in low-Earth orbit at altitudes ranging between 500-2,000km (310-1,242 miles). Starmind's satellites will communicate with Starlink's and then relay the data to Earth. The plans to put data centres in orbit and on the Moon Speaking to the Today programme, on BBC Radio 4, Prof Sir Martin Sweeting, founder and executive chairman of Surrey Satellite Technology Ltd, said while the idea of data centres in space seemed "technically feasible", whether it "makes sense at scale yet" still needed to be analysed. Being able to get the data from the network of satellites, he added, would depend on being able to use laser links from the ground to them. "That has not yet been perfected to the level at which it would be able to support the huge amounts of data that are likely to be transferred backwards and forwards," he said. Meanwhile, the American Astronomical Society (AAS) said it was "disheartened and dismayed" by the decision. It said the proposed constellation would "significantly undermine decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities" as well as "the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky". It noted that the constellation "involves larger (and therefore brighter) and more numerous objects", meaning the satellites would "be visible as extremely bright objects for longer periods in the night sky". Jan Hasselman, a senior attorney at the non-profit group Earthjustice, said in a statement: "Drastically expanding satellites in space has a direct impact on people's everyday lives as well as the future of our planet." Separately, another cautioned that the growing number of low-orbit craft increases the possibility of crashes between objects - which could damage machines or send materials falling back to earth. Starlink has been accused of creating congestion in space, something Musk denies. He has also rejected claims his satellites have been taking up too much room and crowding out competitors. The Federal Communications Commission said on November 25, 2026, that it had "granted the first authorization in U.S. history for a constellation of data centers in space". The order covers SpaceX's planned orbital data-processing network, which is called Starmind. Shares of SpaceX closed at $127.44, up 1.30%, or $1.63, and traded at $128.96 after hours. If it fails to meet those dates, the grant becomes "null and void." The FCC authorization was granted despite objections from Amazon, Viasat, and the American Astronomical Society, which flagged concerns over orbital debris and congestion, radiofrequency interference, and environmental consequences. Amazon, which is building a competitor to SpaceX’s Starlink service, argued in its petition that the application lacked basic details and described it as a “lofty ambition rather than a real plan.” Despite that lack of detail, Amazon also said the proposal “risks real harm.” The FCC dismissed some of the key concerns raised by opponents, including potential threats to scientific research, because the agency determined they fell outside its regulatory authority. FCC Chair Brendan Carr said in a statement that the action “opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth.” Musk thanked Carr in a post on X , writing “Much appreciate. extraction.body: U.S. FCC Approves SpaceX Deployment of 1 Million Satellites for Space Data Centers SpaceX, the space company led by Elon Musk, has received approval from U.S. regulators to place up to 1 million satellites in Earth orbit to build artificial intelligence (AI) data centers. On November 25 (local time), the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said it had approved the launch and operation of satellites for SpaceX's space data center project, "Starmind." This is the first time U.S. regulators have approved the operation of a satellite constellation to build space data centers. The approval came about 10 months after SpaceX submitted its application in January. SpaceX plans to place satellites equipped with AI semiconductors in low Earth orbit and use electricity generated by solar power to process large volumes of data. Data processed in space will be transmitted to Earth via high-speed laser communications and the satellite network of Starlink, SpaceX's satellite internet service. CEO Musk unveiled plans to build space data centers while pursuing a merger between SpaceX and AI company xAI. The plan is based on the view that it could overcome challenges involved in securing the enormous amounts of electricity and water, as well as the land, needed to build data centers on the ground. Musk has previously predicted that space will become the least expensive place to operate AI data centers within the next two to three years. FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said, "Data centers are essential for the United States to maintain its leadership in the field of superintelligence (SI)." He emphasized that the decision would combine the strengths of the U.S. space industry and advanced technology and help strengthen the country's economic leadership. Under the approval, SpaceX must deploy its first satellite by November 2033. It must then deploy 100,000 satellites by November 2035 and 500,000 by November 2038. The deadline for deploying the full constellation is November 2040. However, environmental concerns and technical challenges related to deploying satellites on such a large scale remain. Amazon, competitors, and the American Astronomical Society have raised concerns about the possibility of collisions between satellites, an increase in space debris, and interference with astronomical observations. Despite these objections, the FCC approved SpaceX's satellite constellation without conducting a separate additional environmental impact assessment. However, it deferred approval of SpaceX's request to move some satellites at the end of their operational lives to a separate orbit for disposal, rather than having them reenter the atmosphere, saying that it lacked sufficient information. © The Asia Business Daily. passages: U.S. FCC Approves SpaceX Deployment of 1 Million Satellites for Space Data Centers
SpaceX, the space company led by Elon Musk, has received approval from U.S. regulators to place up to 1 million satellites in Earth orbit to build artificial intelligence (AI) data centers.

On November 25 (local time), the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said it had approved the launch and operation of satellites for SpaceX's space data center project, "Starmind." This is the first time U.S. regulators have approved the operation of a satellite constellation to build space data centers. The approval came about 10 months after SpaceX submitted its application in January.

SpaceX plans to place satellites equipped with AI semiconductors in low Earth orbit and use electricity generated by solar power to process large volumes of data. Data processed in space will be transmitted to Earth via high-speed laser communications and the satellite network of Starlink, SpaceX's satellite internet service.

CEO Musk unveiled plans to build space data centers while pursuing a merger between SpaceX and AI company xAI. The plan is based on the view that it could overcome challenges involved in securing the enormous amounts of electricity and water, as well as the land, needed to build data centers on the ground. Musk has previously predicted that space will become the least expensive place to operate AI data centers within the next two to three years.

FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said, "Data centers are essential for the United States to maintain its leadership in the field of superintelligence (SI)." He emphasized that the decision would combine the strengths of the U.S. space industry and advanced technology and help strengthen the country's economic leadership.

Under the approval, SpaceX must deploy its first satellite by November 2033. It must then deploy 100,000 satellites by November 2035 and 500,000 by November 2038. The deadline for deploying the full constellation is November 2040.

However, environmental concerns and technical challenges related to deploying satellites on such a large scale remain. Amazon, competitors, and the American Astronomical Society have raised concerns about the possibility of collisions between satellites, an increase in space debris, and interference with astronomical observations.

Despite these objections, the FCC approved SpaceX's satellite constellation without conducting a separate additional environmental impact assessment. However, it deferred approval of SpaceX's request to move some satellites at the end of their operational lives to a separate orbit for disposal, rather than having them reenter the atmosphere, saying that it lacked sufficient information.

The Federal Communications Commission said on November 25, 2026, that it had "granted the first authorization in U.S. history for a constellation of data centers in space". sources.title: FCC approves SpaceX plan to put AI data centers in space
passages: SpaceX was given conditional approval by the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday to deploy and operate a constellation of up to 1 million satellites for its orbital data center business, a regulatory victory for Elon Musk and his bid to move AI data centers into space.
The Starmind satellites would primarily communicate using lasers to connect with other satellites, including SpaceX’s Starlink.
The company must also clear other regulatory hurdles.
SpaceX requested a waiver of existing FCC rules, which requires satellites ending missions below 2,000 kilometers reenter Earth’s atmosphere within five years of completing those missions.
The company is interested in moving some of these retired satellites into other orbits around Earth or even around the sun, according to the FCC authorization document .

SpaceX faces a number of technical and economic challenges, including how to dramatically reduce the cost of manufacturing and launching satellites, cool processors in space, and even how to secure financing for chips that are destined for orbit.
The FCC has given SpaceX time to sort out these issues.
Under the approval, SpaceX has seven years to get its first operational satellite into orbit and 14 years to deploy the entire constellation.
