extraction.body: U.S. FCC Approves SpaceX Deployment of 1 Million Satellites for Space Data Centers SpaceX, the space company led by Elon Musk, has received approval from U.S. regulators to place up to 1 million satellites in Earth orbit to build artificial intelligence (AI) data centers. On November 25 (local time), the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said it had approved the launch and operation of satellites for SpaceX's space data center project, "Starmind." This is the first time U.S. regulators have approved the operation of a satellite constellation to build space data centers. The approval came about 10 months after SpaceX submitted its application in January. SpaceX plans to place satellites equipped with AI semiconductors in low Earth orbit and use electricity generated by solar power to process large volumes of data. Data processed in space will be transmitted to Earth via high-speed laser communications and the satellite network of Starlink, SpaceX's satellite internet service. CEO Musk unveiled plans to build space data centers while pursuing a merger between SpaceX and AI company xAI. The plan is based on the view that it could overcome challenges involved in securing the enormous amounts of electricity and water, as well as the land, needed to build data centers on the ground. Musk has previously predicted that space will become the least expensive place to operate AI data centers within the next two to three years. SpaceX, the space company led by Elon Musk, has received approval from U.S. regulators to place up to 1 million satellites in Earth orbit to build artificial intelligence (AI) data centers.

On November 25 (local time), the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said it had approved the launch and operation of satellites for SpaceX's space data center project, "Starmind." This is the first time U.S. regulators have approved the operation of a satellite constellation to build space data centers. The approval came about 10 months after SpaceX submitted its application in January.

SpaceX plans to place satellites equipped with AI semiconductors in low Earth orbit and use electricity generated by solar power to process large volumes of data. Data processed in space will be transmitted to Earth via high-speed laser communications and the satellite network of Starlink, SpaceX's satellite internet service.

CEO Musk unveiled plans to build space data centers while pursuing a merger between SpaceX and AI company xAI. The plan is based on the view that it could overcome challenges involved in securing the enormous amounts of electricity and water, as well as the land, needed to build data centers on the ground. passages: US-listed exchange-traded funds (ETFs) investing in Bitcoin are heading for the worst month of outflows since their 2024 debut, as a persistent sell-off in the world’s largest cryptocurrency drives investors away.
BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust, the largest fund holding the token, has suffered about US$4 billion of redemptions in November , also putting it on course for its worst monthly outflow.
“When a market cannot hold a rally on good news, it usually means that investors are using any strength to sell,” data analytics firm Glassnode said in a note.
“Bitcoin trades round the clock and tends to be one of the first assets sold when investors want less risk.”
The losses underscore a sharp reversal for a group of ETFs that helped propel Bitcoin higher after their US debut in January 2024.

Bitcoin is facing numerous headwinds, from high-profile hacks that have undermined confidence in its security to the prospect of higher interest rates and greater regulatory scrutiny following the recent US midterm elections .

Bitcoin is also facing greater competition for investor capital as money gravitates towards equities and assets offering income, according to Ayesha Kiani, chief operating officer of Monarq Asset Management.
Bitcoin is “competing for the same risk capital that is going into equities right now”, Kiani told Bloomberg Television, describing the ETF exodus as “concerning”.
“There are better yield-bearing assets out there at this point.

US-listed exchange-traded funds (ETFs) investing in Bitcoin are heading for the worst month of outflows since their 2024 debut, as a persistent sell-off in the world’s largest cryptocurrency drives investors away. A net US$4.71 billion (S$6 billion) has been withdrawn from the funds in November so far, according to data compiled by Bloomberg through Nov 23. BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust, the largest fund holding the token, has suffered about US$4 billion of redemptions in November , also putting it on course for its worst monthly outflow. The exodus comes as Bitcoin tumbles below US$60,000 and heads for its worst monthly performance since June 2022, when a string of corporate failures triggered a broader crypto market meltdown. The token has dropped about 23% in November and was trading around US$59,200 as at 1pm on Nov 25 in Singapore, down about 1% in the Asia session. The losses underscore a sharp reversal for a group of ETFs that helped propel Bitcoin higher after their US debut in January 2024. The funds opened the cryptocurrency to a wider pool of institutional and retail investors and became an important source of demand during the bull market. Their record redemptions are now reinforcing the current downturn as that source of buying dries up. Bitcoin briefly recovered alongside other risk assets on Nov 23 after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive, but has since surrendered all of those gains, a sign that investors are using rallies to reduce exposure. “When a market cannot hold a rally on good news, it usually means that investors are using any strength to sell,” data analytics firm Glassnode said in a note. “Bitcoin trades round the clock and tends to be one of the first assets sold when investors want less risk.” Bitcoin is facing numerous headwinds, from high-profile hacks that have undermined confidence in its security to the prospect of higher interest rates and greater regulatory scrutiny following the recent US midterm elections . The absence of US demand is adding to the pressure, according to Glassnode. “The ETFs and other institutions were an important source of demand on the way up, and there is little interest from them at these prices,” the firm said. “A return to ETF inflows, together with net buying on Coinbase, would be the first sign that this is changing.” Bitcoin is also facing greater competition for investor capital as money gravitates towards equities and assets offering income, according to Ayesha Kiani, chief operating officer of Monarq Asset Management. Bitcoin is “competing for the same risk capital that is going into equities right now”, Kiani told Bloomberg Television, describing the ETF exodus as “concerning”. The cryptocurrency industry may need a fresh catalyst to revive demand after the forces that drove the previous rally have faded, she said. “I think we do need to find a new narrative, a new catalyst, a new market, something new for the entire industry for us to become that emerging asset class again,” Kiani said. “There are better yield-bearing assets out there at this point. So, like, why Bitcoin?” BLOOMBERG

extraction.body: X is finally rolling out parental controls that allow parents and guardians to manage teens’ accounts on the platform. “Parents and guardians cannot read private messages, see searches or viewing history, post as their teen, or access the account,” explains the X safety team. A teen and parent / guardian will both have to agree before the controls start. “Supervision on X starts with a handshake and ends automatically when a teen becomes an adult,” says Mridul Singhai, product engineering lead at X. Simple, transparent, and built to grow with families.” The new parental controls come just days after Oregon and Virginia both sued SpaceX over Grok’s porn deepfakes. The complaint in Virginia accuses X owner Elon Musk of willfully ignoring growing concerns around AI-generated sexualized deepfakes, and describes Grok’s weak safeguards as “not a failure but a feature.” Three teens also filed a lawsuit against xAI earlier this year, claiming that Grok generated child sexual abuse material (CSAM) when launching its “spicy mode” last year. Grok was also undressing women and minors earlier this year. X admits its platform isn’t “designed for or promoted to children,” and it already restricts teen accounts to a protected mode, where sensitive media is restricted and targeted advertising is blocked. These latest parental controls may well help teens avoid the very worst parts of X, just as the platform faces more scrutiny from states and regulators.

extraction.body: Digital Trends may earn a commission when you buy through links on our site. Why trust us? Elon Musk-owned X, formerly Twitter, stirred a safety storm a few days when it was discovered that the platform continues to host disturbing material depicting child sexual abuse , and that a network of accounts was promoting services to create non-consensual explicit images . X has just announced a new set of parental safety controls to keep teen users aged 13 to 17 safe on its platform. These changes mirror what rival social media platforms such as Instagram and TikTok have offered for a while now. X notes that parents can now see how much time their teen children have spent on the platform over the past week, and even set daily limits for the platform. Parents can also require approval for every new follower request, which also turns the teen’s account private. Additionally, parents can limit the For You feed, which pushes out algorithmically recommended content, so that it only shows posts and videos from accounts their teen already follows. Parents will also have the option to turn off sensitive media and even filter out specific words that they deem harmful or unfit for users under 18 years of age. They can also control who is allowed to send direct messages to their teen. “Parents want practical tools, and teens deserve room to grow. With Parental Controls on X, families can set the guardrails that fit their home, while teens keep ownership of their accounts and can see every change. Striking that balance is vital and what we set out to build.” Michael O’Herlihy, Head of Safety at X, was quoted as saying. More importantly, X says that parents can now also see who their kids are messaging one-on-one on the platform. Parents won’t be able to see the contents of the messages. However, they will be able to see the contacts, the people who appear in the DMs section, which has now been rebranded to XChat. Parents also can’t see their teen’s searches or viewing history, post on their behalf, or access their account, and every change a parent makes is visible to the teen. Parents will be able to keep an eye on up to five accounts and set safety guardrails on them. Moreover, a teen account can only be linked to one parental account on the platform. Additionally, parental controls will only be enforced when both the parent and the teen explicitly agree to the supervision, and the supervision ends automatically once the teen turns 18. The controls come at a time when social media platforms are facing more heat over safety. Over the past couple of years, the platform has courted plenty of criticism over content safety. According to a report published earlier this year by the Center for Countering Digital Hate (CCDH), X’s algorithm recommends sexually explicit content to accounts belonging to users as young as 13. Researchers from the nonprofit created two accounts posing as 13-year-old users in the UK to check the platform’s content safety, and found that it was pretty easy for them to look up and get exposed to content depicting sexual acts, porn, and more, in both video and still-image formats. UK regulator Ofcom also launched an investigation into X earlier this year to verify whether it complies with the Online Safety Act, following reports that Grok was being used to create sexual deepfakes. During the probe, Ofcom found that in certain cases, age-gated pornographic content remained accessible to accounts that had not been verified as belonging to adults, after which X made changes to restrict that content. In September, Ireland’s media watchdog launched an investigation into the platform over concerns that its age checks were not effectively preventing children from accessing pornographic and violent content, and questioned whether X’s parental controls met the minimum requirements. This week, Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield and Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones sued X and other Musk companies, alleging that the integrated Grok AI chatbot helped proliferate non-consensual sexual images and child sexual abuse material on the site. Birthday wishes and reminders can now go out right on the minute You think of the perfect birthday message at midnight, or a good-luck text for tomorrow's job interview at 10pm, and you hold off because sending it right now would feel odd. WhatsApp has finally built a way around that dilemma. On November 25, the company announced scheduled messages and called the feature one of its most requested, with a rollout that covers both iPhone and Android. Static memes and looping animations are popular ways to express yourself in busy chat groups. While these have completely remained silent, a new upcoming feature could be a bit noisy, as WhatsApp reportedly plans to bring custom stickers that play audio right inside your conversations. A new report by WABetaInfo says that the messaging app is pushing sound sticker messages to select Android beta testers after months of internal testing. Back in October, WhatsApp was spotted testing sound stickers in early preview builds before regular testers could try them out. Now the feature is finally reaching real accounts, turning short clips from your phone gallery into shareable reactions with sound for anyone who spends time in WhatsApp threads every day; it lands right between a quick reaction meme and a full voice message. Australia has just passed the landmark Digital Duty of Care law, which gives users more power over social media platforms when it comes to digital harm. The law also lays out a provision for imposing fines as high as 5% of a platform's global revenue, a sharp jump from the originally proposed cap of A$109.2 million (roughly $72 million). The key objective of the law is to protect users online, especially children, from harmful content and features such as gender-based violence, nudification services, behaviorally addictive design, and more. One of the most remarkable aspects of the law is the private right of action, which allows an individual to directly sue companies for breaching their duty of care. And it's not just social media. On the contrary, the law also covers search engines, app stores, hosting tools, and even AI services that generate content. The law also requires platforms to comply with content removal notices within 24 hours, down from 48 hours, or face penalties worth millions of dollars. Social media platforms, of course, are not happy, telling The Guardian that private right to sue is complex and can ultimately prove to be counter-productive. extraction.body: Subject in the field of online media; media identifier - R40-05926 This resource is intended for persons who have reached the age of 21. X has allowed parents to control teenagers’ time on the platform, content, and followers. Access to messages and search history will remain restricted. Elon Musk's X has "finally" introduced parental control features for children aged 13 to 17, allowing parents and guardians to manage their teenagers' use of the platform. Engadget reports, UNN writes. Teen accounts will now be in protected mode by default, with restricted access to sensitive content and targeted advertising blocked. The new settings will also provide families with "additional tools on top of these default settings," the platform announced. These additional tools allow adults responsible for teenagers to see how much time their children spend on X and set a daily limit, require approval for new followers, and limit "For You" recommendations to only those accounts the teenager already follows. They can also filter certain words, disable sensitive media content, allow parents to control who can send direct messages, and see which accounts their teenager has communicated with one-on-one (without seeing the messages themselves). To use the new parental control features, users must follow the instructions in X's Help Center. "The connection starts with the parent or guardian and ends with the teenager. Both users must agree," the platform states. X emphasized that the new controls allow parents to manage content without intruding on their children's lives. "Parents and guardians cannot read direct messages, view search or browsing history, post on behalf of their teenager, or access the account," the company wrote. Parents will be able to control up to five teen accounts. "Although the X platform is not intended for children and is not marketed to them, and users must be at least 13 years old where required by law, we take particular care with young people who are here," the company wrote. Stating that "child safety is X's top priority," the platform likely introduced the new rules to comply with current or forthcoming regulations in several states and countries, the publication writes. extraction.body: X is finally rolling out parental controls that allow parents and guardians to manage teens’ accounts on the platform. “Parents and guardians cannot read private messages, see searches or viewing history, post as their teen, or access the account,” explains the X safety team. A teen and parent / guardian will both have to agree before the controls start. “Supervision on X starts with a handshake and ends automatically when a teen becomes an adult,” says Mridul Singhai, product engineering lead at X. Simple, transparent, and built to grow with families.” The new parental controls come just days after Oregon and Virginia both sued SpaceX over Grok’s porn deepfakes. The complaint in Virginia accuses X owner Elon Musk of willfully ignoring growing concerns around AI-generated sexualized deepfakes, and describes Grok’s weak safeguards as “not a failure but a feature.” Three teens also filed a lawsuit against xAI earlier this year, claiming that Grok generated child sexual abuse material (CSAM) when launching its “spicy mode” last year. Grok was also undressing women and minors earlier this year. X admits its platform isn’t “designed for or promoted to children,” and it already restricts teen accounts to a protected mode, where sensitive media is restricted and targeted advertising is blocked. These latest parental controls may well help teens avoid the very worst parts of X, just as the platform faces more scrutiny from states and regulators.

Elon Musk-owned X, formerly Twitter, stirred a safety storm a few days when it was discovered that the platform continues to host disturbing material depicting child sexual abuse , and that a network of accounts was promoting services to create non-consensual explicit images . X has just announced a new set of parental safety controls to keep teen users aged 13 to 17 safe on its platform. These changes mirror what rival social media platforms such as Instagram and TikTok have offered for a while now. X notes that parents can now see how much time their teen children have spent on the platform over the past week, and even set daily limits for the platform. Parents can also require approval for every new follower request, which also turns the teen’s account private. Additionally, parents can limit the For You feed, which pushes out algorithmically recommended content, so that it only shows posts and videos from accounts their teen already follows. Parents will also have the option to turn off sensitive media and even filter out specific words that they deem harmful or unfit for users under 18 years of age. They can also control who is allowed to send direct messages to their teen. “Parents want practical tools, and teens deserve room to grow. With Parental Controls on X, families can set the guardrails that fit their home, while teens keep ownership of their accounts and can see every change. Striking that balance is vital and what we set out to build.” Michael O’Herlihy, Head of Safety at X, was quoted as saying. More importantly, X says that parents can now also see who their kids are messaging one-on-one on the platform. Parents won’t be able to see the contents of the messages. However, they will be able to see the contacts, the people who appear in the DMs section, which has now been rebranded to XChat. Parents also can’t see their teen’s searches or viewing history, post on their behalf, or access their account, and every change a parent makes is visible to the teen. Parents will be able to keep an eye on up to five accounts and set safety guardrails on them. Moreover, a teen account can only be linked to one parental account on the platform. Additionally, parental controls will only be enforced when both the parent and the teen explicitly agree to the supervision, and the supervision ends automatically once the teen turns 18. The controls come at a time when social media platforms are facing more heat over safety. Over the past couple of years, the platform has courted plenty of criticism over content safety. According to a report published earlier this year by the Center for Countering Digital Hate (CCDH), X’s algorithm recommends sexually explicit content to accounts belonging to users as young as 13. Researchers from the nonprofit created two accounts posing as 13-year-old users in the UK to check the platform’s content safety, and found that it was pretty easy for them to look up and get exposed to content depicting sexual acts, porn, and more, in both video and still-image formats. UK regulator Ofcom also launched an investigation into X earlier this year to verify whether it complies with the Online Safety Act, following reports that Grok was being used to create sexual deepfakes. During the probe, Ofcom found that in certain cases, age-gated pornographic content remained accessible to accounts that had not been verified as belonging to adults, after which X made changes to restrict that content. In September, Ireland’s media watchdog launched an investigation into the platform over concerns that its age checks were not effectively preventing children from accessing pornographic and violent content, and questioned whether X’s parental controls met the minimum requirements. This week, Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield and Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones sued X and other Musk companies, alleging that the integrated Grok AI chatbot helped proliferate non-consensual sexual images and child sexual abuse material on the site. Birthday wishes and reminders can now go out right on the minute You think of the perfect birthday message at midnight, or a good-luck text for tomorrow's job interview at 10pm, and you hold off because sending it right now would feel odd. WhatsApp has finally built a way around that dilemma. On November 25, the company announced scheduled messages and called the feature one of its most requested, with a rollout that covers both iPhone and Android. Static memes and looping animations are popular ways to express yourself in busy chat groups. While these have completely remained silent, a new upcoming feature could be a bit noisy, as WhatsApp reportedly plans to bring custom stickers that play audio right inside your conversations. A new report by WABetaInfo says that the messaging app is pushing sound sticker messages to select Android beta testers after months of internal testing. Back in October, WhatsApp was spotted testing sound stickers in early preview builds before regular testers could try them out. Now the feature is finally reaching real accounts, turning short clips from your phone gallery into shareable reactions with sound for anyone who spends time in WhatsApp threads every day; it lands right between a quick reaction meme and a full voice message. Australia has just passed the landmark Digital Duty of Care law, which gives users more power over social media platforms when it comes to digital harm. The law also lays out a provision for imposing fines as high as 5% of a platform's global revenue, a sharp jump from the originally proposed cap of A$109.2 million (roughly $72 million). The key objective of the law is to protect users online, especially children, from harmful content and features such as gender-based violence, nudification services, behaviorally addictive design, and more. One of the most remarkable aspects of the law is the private right of action, which allows an individual to directly sue companies for breaching their duty of care. And it's not just social media. On the contrary, the law also covers search engines, app stores, hosting tools, and even AI services that generate content. The law also requires platforms to comply with content removal notices within 24 hours, down from 48 hours, or face penalties worth millions of dollars. Social media platforms, of course, are not happy, telling The Guardian that private right to sue is complex and can ultimately prove to be counter-productive. X notes that parents can now see how much time their teen children have spent on the platform over the past week, and even set daily limits for the platform. Parents can also require approval for every new follower request, which also turns the teen’s account private. Additionally, parents can limit the For You feed, which pushes out algorithmically recommended content, so that it only shows posts and videos from accounts their teen already follows.

Parents will also have the option to turn off sensitive media and even filter out specific words that they deem harmful or unfit for users under 18 years of age. They can also control who is allowed to send direct messages to their teen. “Parents want practical tools, and teens deserve room to grow. With Parental Controls on X, families can set the guardrails that fit their home, while teens keep ownership of their accounts and can see every change. Striking that balance is vital and what we set out to build.” Michael O’Herlihy, Head of Safety at X, was quoted as saying.

More importantly, X says that parents can now also see who their kids are messaging one-on-one on the platform. Parents won’t be able to see the contents of the messages. However, they will be able to see the contacts, the people who appear in the DMs section, which has now been rebranded to XChat. Parents also can’t see their teen’s searches or viewing history, post on their behalf, or access their account, and every change a parent makes is visible to the teen.

Parents will be able to keep an eye on up to five accounts and set safety guardrails on them. Moreover, a teen account can only be linked to one parental account on the platform. Additionally, parental controls will only be enforced when both the parent and the teen explicitly agree to the supervision, and the supervision ends automatically once the teen turns 18. The controls come at a time when social media platforms are facing more heat over safety.

Over the past couple of years, the platform has courted plenty of criticism over content safety. According to a report published earlier this year by the Center for Countering Digital Hate (CCDH), X’s algorithm recommends sexually explicit content to accounts belonging to users as young as 13. Researchers from the nonprofit created two accounts posing as 13-year-old users in the UK to check the platform’s content safety, and found that it was pretty easy for them to look up and get exposed to content depicting sexual acts, porn, and more, in both video and still-image formats.

UK regulator Ofcom also launched an investigation into X earlier this year to verify whether it complies with the Online Safety Act, following reports that Grok was being used to create sexual deepfakes. During the probe, Ofcom found that in certain cases, age-gated pornographic content remained accessible to accounts that had not been verified as belonging to adults, after which X made changes to restrict that content.

In September, Ireland’s media watchdog launched an investigation into the platform over concerns that its age checks were not effectively preventing children from accessing pornographic and violent content, and questioned whether X’s parental controls met the minimum requirements. This week, Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield and Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones sued X and other Musk companies, alleging that the integrated Grok AI chatbot helped proliferate non-consensual sexual images and child sexual abuse material on the site.
Birthday wishes and reminders can now go out right on the minute

You think of the perfect birthday message at midnight, or a good-luck text for tomorrow's job interview at 10pm, and you hold off because sending it right now would feel odd. WhatsApp has finally built a way around that dilemma. On November 25, the company announced scheduled messages and called the feature one of its most requested, with a rollout that covers both iPhone and Android.

Static memes and looping animations are popular ways to express yourself in busy chat groups. While these have completely remained silent, a new upcoming feature could be a bit noisy, as WhatsApp reportedly plans to bring custom stickers that play audio right inside your conversations. A new report by WABetaInfo says that the messaging app is pushing sound sticker messages to select Android beta testers after months of internal testing.

Back in October, WhatsApp was spotted testing sound stickers in early preview builds before regular testers could try them out. Now the feature is finally reaching real accounts, turning short clips from your phone gallery into shareable reactions with sound for anyone who spends time in WhatsApp threads every day; it lands right between a quick reaction meme and a full voice message.

Australia has just passed the landmark Digital Duty of Care law, which gives users more power over social media platforms when it comes to digital harm. The law also lays out a provision for imposing fines as high as 5% of a platform's global revenue, a sharp jump from the originally proposed cap of A$109.2 million (roughly $72 million). The key objective of the law is to protect users online, especially children, from harmful content and features such as gender-based violence, nudification services, behaviorally addictive design, and more.

One of the most remarkable aspects of the law is the private right of action, which allows an individual to directly sue companies for breaching their duty of care. And it's not just social media. On the contrary, the law also covers search engines, app stores, hosting tools, and even AI services that generate content. The law also requires platforms to comply with content removal notices within 24 hours, down from 48 hours, or face penalties worth millions of dollars. Social media platforms, of course, are not happy, telling The Guardian that private right to sue is complex and can ultimately prove to be counter-productive.

sources.title: YouTube Shorts finally adds daily time limit. Here's how to get it.
passages: According to the annual report, 73 percent of teens say they visit YouTube daily, with 15 percent describing their use as "almost constant." The survey also found the majority of Americans support time limits for minors on social media, which comes as no surprise considering the ongoing legal battles facing Big Tech.YouTube is currently facing multiple lawsuits alongside Meta's Facebook and Instagram, TikTok, and Snapchat, over their social media platforms' roles in the ongoing youth mental health crisis.

For parents, YouTube said it's planning to add the Shorts time limit to the app's parental controls to incorporate "later this year," which will give parents and guardians controlling supervised accounts the ability to turn the setting on and make it non-dismissible.
If you're looking to chop your YouTube Shorts time, there's a way to curb your doomscrolling.

YouTube has added tools over the years including take a break and bedtime reminders as well as a sleep timer, but this one's especially made for Shorts."Setting a scrolling time limit on the Shorts feed allows for this exploration while helping users be more deliberate about their viewing habits and manage their time effectively," reads a blog post by YouTube owner Google.
However, at the same time, YouTube Shorts has added longer form videos and more TikTok-like editing tools, expanding the capabilities of the site to serve up more screen time-tempting content.
22, YouTube announced a new setting for Shorts which lets you set a daily viewing limit.

The breach, detected by Zodia on Monday, resulted in some client and staff data, including names and email addresses, being leaked, Zodia Custody CEO Richard Clark said in an emailed statement. The company's London-listed shares were up 2.6 per cent on the day. "Based on our investigation to date, there have been no unauthorised transactions," Clark said. extraction.body: Institutional cryptocurrency custodian Zodia Custody has suffered a security breach that exposed personal information belonging to some of its clients and employees. Zodia Custody detected a security breach on Nov. 23 that exposed personal information belonging to some of its clients and employees. CEO Richard Clark confirmed that the compromised information included names and email addresses in an emailed statement to Reuters. The incident follows Standard Chartered’s Oct. 21 announcement of definitive agreements to acquire full ownership of the institutional crypto custodian. Shares of Standard Chartered were trading 2.6% higher in London on Thursday. In an emailed statement to Reuters on Thursday, Nov. 26, Zodia Custody CEO Richard Clark confirmed that the company had detected the breach on Monday, Nov. 23, and that the information exposed included names and email addresses. Shares of Standard Chartered, which has been working to bring Zodia Custody’s operations into its international banking business, were trading 2.6% higher in London on Thursday. Founded in 2020 through a partnership between Standard Chartered and Northern Trust, Zodia Custody caters primarily to institutional investors, including financial institutions, asset managers, and hedge funds. The business has since attracted investment from several major banks, including Japan’s SBI Holdings, National Australia Bank, and Emirates NBD. How Zodia Custody handles institutional assets Zodia Custody operates a segregated custody model, under which digital assets belonging to individual clients are held in separate wallets according to their instructions. According to the company's custody policy, its core storage infrastructure keeps cryptographic keys offline, with transactions requiring multiple independent approvals and authentication checks before assets can be withdrawn. Alongside its cold storage infrastructure, the custodian offers a separate solution based on multi-party computation, where the cryptographic information required to authorize transactions is distributed across multiple secure environments instead of being held in one location. Earlier this month, Clark told crypto.news that financial institutions using tokenized assets as collateral need infrastructure that allows them to move assets continuously while retaining the protections associated with institutional custody. His comments addressed the growing use of tokenized assets as collateral, particularly in financing arrangements where institutions may otherwise have to release assets from custody before completing a transaction. Zodia operates its own institutional settlement network, Interchange, through which customers can access trading, lending, and borrowing services while keeping their digital assets in custody until settlement. Standard Chartered moves to consolidate its crypto custody business The security incident follows Standard Chartered’s Oct. 21 announcement that it had entered into definitive agreements to acquire the entirety of Zodia Custody through its subsidiary, Standard Chartered I H Limited. extraction.body: Institutional cryptocurrency custodian Zodia Custody has suffered a security breach that exposed personal information belonging to some of its clients and employees. Zodia Custody detected a security breach on Nov. 23 that exposed personal information belonging to some of its clients and employees. CEO Richard Clark confirmed that the compromised information included names and email addresses in an emailed statement to Reuters. The incident follows Standard Chartered’s Oct. 21 announcement of definitive agreements to acquire full ownership of the institutional crypto custodian. Shares of Standard Chartered were trading 2.6% higher in London on Thursday. In an emailed statement to Reuters on Thursday, Nov. 26, Zodia Custody CEO Richard Clark confirmed that the company had detected the breach on Monday, Nov. 23, and that the information exposed included names and email addresses. Shares of Standard Chartered, which has been working to bring Zodia Custody’s operations into its international banking business, were trading 2.6% higher in London on Thursday. Founded in 2020 through a partnership between Standard Chartered and Northern Trust, Zodia Custody caters primarily to institutional investors, including financial institutions, asset managers, and hedge funds. The business has since attracted investment from several major banks, including Japan’s SBI Holdings, National Australia Bank, and Emirates NBD. How Zodia Custody handles institutional assets Zodia Custody operates a segregated custody model, under which digital assets belonging to individual clients are held in separate wallets according to their instructions. According to the company's custody policy, its core storage infrastructure keeps cryptographic keys offline, with transactions requiring multiple independent approvals and authentication checks before assets can be withdrawn. Alongside its cold storage infrastructure, the custodian offers a separate solution based on multi-party computation, where the cryptographic information required to authorize transactions is distributed across multiple secure environments instead of being held in one location. Earlier this month, Clark told crypto.news that financial institutions using tokenized assets as collateral need infrastructure that allows them to move assets continuously while retaining the protections associated with institutional custody. His comments addressed the growing use of tokenized assets as collateral, particularly in financing arrangements where institutions may otherwise have to release assets from custody before completing a transaction. Zodia operates its own institutional settlement network, Interchange, through which customers can access trading, lending, and borrowing services while keeping their digital assets in custody until settlement. Standard Chartered moves to consolidate its crypto custody business The security incident follows Standard Chartered’s Oct. 21 announcement that it had entered into definitive agreements to acquire the entirety of Zodia Custody through its subsidiary, Standard Chartered I H Limited. The bank first secured the acceptance of its nonbinding acquisition offer from Zodia’s shareholders and noteholders in May, with the parties initially expecting to finalize their agreements by the end of June and complete the transaction before the end of August. As part of the revised acquisition arrangement, Zodia’s regulated operations across Singapore, Hong Kong, Australia, the United Arab Emirates, and Luxembourg are to become part of Standard Chartered’s Securities Services division, which already provides custody for traditional financial instruments and digital assets. Meanwhile, the custodian’s software development and professional services operations are being separated into an independent company called Zodia Solutions under SC Ventures, Standard Chartered’s investment and innovation arm. Led by Craig Perrin, the new business will supply digital asset infrastructure to financial institutions, including Standard Chartered itself, and will retain the backing of several existing Zodia investors. Zodia has expanded its regulated custody operations Over the past year, Zodia Custody has secured several regulatory permissions that allow it to handle financial instruments beyond conventional cryptocurrencies. In June, its European subsidiary obtained a payment institution license from Luxembourg’s Commission de Surveillance du Secteur Financier, allowing it to offer regulated transfer services for electronic money tokens alongside its existing crypto asset safekeeping business. The authorization complements the company's Markets in Crypto-Assets license, which it received in December 2025 and which allows it to provide regulated cryptocurrency custody services across European Union member states. 12, Zodia announced that Abu Dhabi Global Market’s Financial Services Regulatory Authority had expanded the license held by its regional subsidiary, Tungsten Custody Solutions Limited, to cover the custody of digital securities.

Zodia disclosed that a breach exposed limited organization details and some client and employee contact information.
The company said its investigation had found no unauthorized transactions so far.
The incident raises phishing concerns as exposed names and email addresses could aid impersonation attempts.

A crypto custodian can keep private keys offline and still face a security headache. The Zodia Custody data breach exposed limited client and employee information, putting contact details, not confirmed crypto assets, at the centre of the incident.

Zodia detected attempts to probe its systems on November 23 and temporarily took offline software connecting institutional clients directly to its platform. But, the service has since been restored. CEO Richard Clark confirmed the breach on November 26.

The company determined on November 24 that an unauthorized party had accessed limited information. This included organization details and, for a small number of clients and employees, business contact names and email addresses.
But, that’s enough to create another problem. Exposed names paired with working email addresses can help attackers craft convincing phishing messages impersonating Zodia or its staff.
However, the company said its investigation had found no unauthorized transactions so far. Its custody model keeps primary cryptographic keys offline and requires multiple approvals for withdrawals.
There is no confirmation in the disclosed information that client holdings or wallet keys were accessed.
Zodia has notified affected clients and regulators. The incident comes weeks after Standard Chartered increased its stake to 100%, bringing the custody business into its digital asset operations.
Standard Chartered shares listed in London rose 2.6% on November 26, the day the breach was reported. That market move doesn’t answer the questions facing affected customers.

The Zodia Custody data breach makes targeted impersonation a practical concern. Clients should treat unexpected messages requesting withdrawal changes or transfer approvals with suspicion, and verify requests through contact details already held on file.

The investigation’s findings still remain limited. But, how many people were really affected, and whether additional information was accessed or not. Also, how the intrusion occurred have still not been disclosed yet.

Britain is preparing to tighten its oversight of decentralized finance (DeFi), with the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) seeking to bring blockchain-based financial services under its proposed crypto authorization regime. The plans could restrict retail investors from accessing certain decentralized trading platforms, even when those services operate without a central controlling entity. The regulator’s approach differs from those taken by the United States and the European Union. Under the proposed framework, retail equity transactions would have to pass through regulated platforms. The requirement would apply to conventional shares as well as tokenized equities, preventing regulated intermediaries from routing British retail orders to unauthorized offshore DeFi platforms. Jamie Bell, the FCA’s head of capital markets, explained that representing securities on a blockchain should not change their regulatory treatment. The proposals come amid rising deployment of tokenized stocks across decentralized financial applications. Research published by DWF Labs in October estimated that the value of tokenized equities deployed across these applications reached approximately $313 million on October 15, up from $15.5 million at the beginning of the year. According to an FT report, the FCA intends to require authorization for DeFi platforms despite their decentralized operating structures. Officials cited fraud, scams and money laundering among their concerns, noting that consumers have limited options for recovering stolen funds or obtaining compensation. DeFi platforms typically use automated smart contracts to ease trading, borrowing and lending rather than relying on the intermediaries found in traditional financial markets. The regulator also cited October’s $6.3 billion Binance hack , saying stolen assets passed through decentralized exchanges before being converted into other tokens that were harder to trace. Jane Moore, the FCA’s head of department for payments and digital assets, said the speed and scale of such transfers can complicate efforts to freeze stolen funds. She called for industry solutions to address money laundering and raised concerns about operational resilience. The FCA’s proposed approach has drawn criticism from industry representatives, particularly over how broadly the regulator intends to define businesses involved in decentralized finance. Aave Labs’ chief legal and policy officer, Linda Jeng, described the FCA’s position as “highly problematic.” In a letter to the regulator, she sought clarification on whether businesses providing services such as transaction-fee information and sanctions screening could fall under the proposed authorization requirements. Jeng argued that regulation should target the appropriate points in the technology stack rather than impose obligations on businesses that help secure decentralized protocols. Meanwhile, former British Chancellor George Osborne, who advises Coinbase, raised concerns about the restrictions on regulated intermediaries. He suggested these firms could act as gatekeepers connecting customers to decentralized financial markets. Preventing them from directing retail investors to unauthorized DeFi platforms could therefore restrict access to those services. Unlike centralized exchanges, where operators can intervene and freeze customer accounts, many decentralized platforms execute transactions through automated smart contracts, with users retaining control of their assets through self-custodial wallets. Jane Moore, head of payments and digital assets at the FCA, said the speed at which stolen cryptocurrencies move through decentralized platforms can complicate efforts to intercept transactions. She called on the industry to develop solutions capable of addressing such money laundering risks. The regulator had already opened two related consultations on Oct. 21 to establish how businesses using decentralized protocols should comply with financial crime and operational resilience requirements. coreStoryFacts.text: FCA planning ‘strict rules’ for DeFi crypto markets

The UK’s financial regulator is planning to implement restrictions on the decentralised finance (DeFi) cryptocurrency sector that are tighter than those currently deployed by either the EU or the US, it has told the Financial Times.
In today's complex financial landscape, the integration of people, technology, and data is paramount for effective risk management.
Despite this, recent FStech research reveals that only 34 per cent of firms have achieved full integration, whilst 63 per cent are still navigating this crucial journey.
Early challengers like Monzo now mimic banks on the high street.

Revolut has expanded into a financial services provider of everything from bank accounts to crypto wallets, and new challengers from other markets are cashing in on customer loyalty, hoping to expand.
FStech senior reporter Isaac Hanson explores how things have changed, and where they might go from here.

As recent developments from OpenAI, Mastercard and Visa lay the groundwork for a future where AI agents can shop, compare and purchase goods on behalf of consumers, FStech news editor Alexandra Leonards explores the role financial institutions will play in this emerging ecosystem – the opportunities it could unlock, and the complex fraud challenges it may introduce as agentic commerce comes to life

Ahead of his keynote presentation opening FStech’s The Future of AI in Financial Services Doug Robertson, Group Head of Responsible AI Management & Strategy at HSBC speaks exclusively to us about why responsible AI is an accelerator rather than a brake
FStech’s senior reporter Silvia Iacovcich asks experts what they think will be the main challenges for both banks and consumers as the project progresses
FCA issues statement on use of AI agents in UK finance

Britain is preparing to tighten its oversight of decentralized finance (DeFi), with the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) seeking to bring blockchain-based financial services under its proposed crypto authorization regime. The plans could restrict retail investors from accessing certain decentralized trading platforms, even when those services operate without a central controlling entity. The regulator’s approach differs from those taken by the United States and the European Union. Under the proposed framework, retail equity transactions would have to pass through regulated platforms. The requirement would apply to conventional shares as well as tokenized equities, preventing regulated intermediaries from routing British retail orders to unauthorized offshore DeFi platforms. Jamie Bell, the FCA’s head of capital markets, explained that representing securities on a blockchain should not change their regulatory treatment. The proposals come amid rising deployment of tokenized stocks across decentralized financial applications. Research published by DWF Labs in October estimated that the value of tokenized equities deployed across these applications reached approximately $313 million on October 15, up from $15.5 million at the beginning of the year. According to an FT report, the FCA intends to require authorization for DeFi platforms despite their decentralized operating structures. Officials cited fraud, scams and money laundering among their concerns, noting that consumers have limited options for recovering stolen funds or obtaining compensation. DeFi platforms typically use automated smart contracts to ease trading, borrowing and lending rather than relying on the intermediaries found in traditional financial markets. The regulator also cited October’s $6.3 billion Binance hack , saying stolen assets passed through decentralized exchanges before being converted into other tokens that were harder to trace. Jane Moore, the FCA’s head of department for payments and digital assets, said the speed and scale of such transfers can complicate efforts to freeze stolen funds. She called for industry solutions to address money laundering and raised concerns about operational resilience. The FCA’s proposed approach has drawn criticism from industry representatives, particularly over how broadly the regulator intends to define businesses involved in decentralized finance. Aave Labs’ chief legal and policy officer, Linda Jeng, described the FCA’s position as “highly problematic.” In a letter to the regulator, she sought clarification on whether businesses providing services such as transaction-fee information and sanctions screening could fall under the proposed authorization requirements. Jeng argued that regulation should target the appropriate points in the technology stack rather than impose obligations on businesses that help secure decentralized protocols. Meanwhile, former British Chancellor George Osborne, who advises Coinbase, raised concerns about the restrictions on regulated intermediaries. He suggested these firms could act as gatekeepers connecting customers to decentralized financial markets. Preventing them from directing retail investors to unauthorized DeFi platforms could therefore restrict access to those services. The regulator cited the $6.3 billion Binance hack and difficulties recovering stolen funds transferred through decentralized exchanges as reasons for tighter oversight. Proposed rules would prevent regulated intermediaries from routing retail tokenized equity orders to unauthorized offshore DeFi platforms. 26 Financial Times report, the regulator intends to bring a range of blockchain-based financial services within its upcoming regulatory framework, including platforms designed to operate without a central controlling entity. Unlike centralized exchanges, where operators can intervene and freeze customer accounts, many decentralized platforms execute transactions through automated smart contracts, with users retaining control of their assets through self-custodial wallets. Binance hack fuels FCA concerns over DeFi Regulators specifically pointed to the Oct. 29 security breach at Binance, which affected approximately $6.3 billion in digital assets, as an example of how decentralized platforms can be used to move stolen funds. Blockchain intelligence firm Elliptic had identified approximately 1,650 Bitcoin worth $124 million that attackers had acquired by converting other stolen cryptocurrencies as of Nov. 6, as crypto.news previously reported in its coverage of the laundering activity. Jane Moore, head of payments and digital assets at the FCA, said the speed at which stolen cryptocurrencies move through decentralized platforms can complicate efforts to intercept transactions. She called on the industry to develop solutions capable of addressing such money laundering risks. The regulator had already opened two related consultations on Oct. 21 to establish how businesses using decentralized protocols should comply with financial crime and operational resilience requirements. UK plans restrictions on retail tokenized stock trading Under the FCA’s proposed approach, retail orders for equities would have to be executed through regulated platforms regardless of whether investors purchase conventional shares or their blockchain-based equivalents. The requirement would prevent regulated intermediaries from routing British retail investors’ tokenized equity orders to unauthorized offshore DeFi platforms. Jamie Bell, head of capital markets at the FCA, explained that the regulatory treatment of securities should not differ simply because the underlying financial instrument is represented on a blockchain. Research published by DWF Labs in October estimated that approximately $313 million worth of tokenized equities were deployed across decentralized financial applications as of Oct. 15, compared with just $15.5 million at the beginning of the year. Aave and Coinbase challenge the FCA’s approach Linda Jeng, chief legal and policy officer at Aave Labs, described the regulator’s position as “highly problematic” and has written to the FCA seeking clarification over which businesses would be classified as DeFi service providers. Her concerns extend to companies that supply transaction fee information or conduct sanctions screening, with Jeng arguing against imposing regulatory requirements on services that help secure decentralized protocols. Former British Chancellor George Osborne, who advises cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase, argued that regulated intermediaries could serve as gatekeepers between customers and decentralized financial markets. European regulators are examining a similar model. The European Securities and Markets Authority has proposed allowing cryptocurrency exchanges to facilitate access to DeFi services under specific regulatory arrangements. 25, the European Banking Authority separately called for an assessment of additional regulatory requirements for cryptocurrency service providers that connect customers with decentralized lending platforms. When will the UK's new crypto rules take effect? 25, 2027, bringing activities such as cryptocurrency trading, custody, and staking within the FCA’s financial services remit. 28, 2027, to submit their authorization applications. The FCA has offered limited flexibility to firms that can demonstrate that uncertainty over the proposed technical service exemptions affected their ability to complete certain application requirements.

Instead of trying to force crypto into a traditional mold, the FCA is finally acknowledging that this sector requires a unique approach.

The UK’s Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) has published a consultation paper outlining proposals to regulate cryptoasset service providers under a flexible regime. These proposals aim to adjust traditional financial rules to better align with the unique nature of digital assets, including decentralized technologies like blockchain . In a move signaling the UK’s intent to become a crypto-friendly jurisdiction, the FCA has acknowledged that a rigid application of traditional finance rules will not work for digital assets. David Geale, the FCA’s executive director for payments and digital finance, emphasized that while similar risks should result in similar regulatory outcomes, “some of these things are very different.” Instead of a simple copy-paste approach from traditional finance, the new proposals adjust standards to reflect the nature of the crypto market: Despite relaxing some rules, the FCA is also introducing new standards to address crypto-specific risks: Geale reassured that the FCA does not intend to lower overall regulatory standards. He highlighted the importance of ensuring users are fully aware of the risks involved in crypto investing. “We need to always be very clear that this is high risk,” he said. You get one weekly briefing with only the stories that matter. If the market is quiet, we skip it. The consultation follows draft legislation from His Majesty’s Treasury introduced in April, which outlined how crypto exchanges , dealers, and agents would be brought into the fold of financial regulation. The UK government described the initiative as a message that the country is “open for business” but closed to fraud and abuse . In parallel, the UK is working to strengthen international coordination , particularly with the United States. According to the Financial Times, UK Chancellor Rachel Reeves and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent recently discussed deepening crypto cooperation. The meeting reportedly involved leaders from companies such as Coinbase , Circle, and Ripple , along with executives from traditional financial institutions like Bank of America, Barclays, and Citi. In my experience covering crypto regulation, this is one of the most balanced moves we’ve seen from a major financial regulator. Instead of trying to force crypto into a traditional mold, the FCA is finally acknowledging that this sector requires a unique approach. I found their willingness to waive outdated rules while still addressing real risks like cyberattacks and transparency particularly smart. This is how you encourage innovation without letting the wild west run unchecked . It also sends a strong message: the UK is ready to lead on crypto, but not without rules that make sense. extraction.body: What happens to your private conversations when an AI company goes bankrupt ? If it’s Character.ai, apparently, the plan is to auction them off to the highest bidder. Now, a coalition of 42 state attorneys general is intervening in Character.ai’s bankruptcy proceedings in an effort to stop the chatbot maker from selling off sensitive user data, which includes the private conversations of millions of users. The attorneys general involved in the matter have put out individual press releases , claiming that Character.ai’s dataset includes chat histories from more than 21 million U.S. accounts, more than 2.1 million of which belong to minors. In addition, the sale would involve other personal data, like IP addresses, the statements said. Only one anonymous bidder for the chat data has been disclosed so far: Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC (Smirks), which was set up as a Delaware company on November 13, 2026. The following day, Character.ai picked it as the base bid for the auction, scheduled for December 1, California Attorney General Rob Bonta noted . It is unclear what the buyer’s plans are for the chats. In addition, some states, including California, Colorado, New York, and Connecticut, have enacted chatbot safety legislation that will go into effect on January 1, 2027, which could trigger further violations if the sale goes through. “Character.AI promised consumers that their data would not be sold. This kind of behavior is illegal under federal and California law and bankruptcy should not be used to sidestep these consumer protections,” Bonta said in a statement. Connecticut Attorney General William Tong also criticized Character.ai’s business model. “Their chatbots drove vulnerable youth down a rabbit hole of emotionally volatile and sexually inappropriate chats,” Tong said . “Their reckless misconduct and broken business model drove their company into the ground. Now they want to abuse the bankruptcy process to do exactly what they said they wouldn’t do — auction off those private chat records and personal details to a shady buyer.” Tong added: “We objected to the Disney sale, and we’re calling on the bankruptcy court to reject this sale too as yet another guise to eviscerate legal liability and consumer protection.” The opposition to the Disney sale was led by a similar but not identical coalition of state AGs. They fought against a proposed $20 million licensing deal that would give Disney access to Character.ai’s intellectual property, but not to users’ chats. The deal has not yet received final court approval. (Disney also agreed to hire most of Character.ai’s remaining staff .) Character.ai suffered after its co-founders, Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, returned to Google , when the tech giant signed a non-exclusive license to use the AI startup’s tech. The company also faced lawsuits related to child safety — one involved the suicide of a 14-year-old Florida boy whose mother claimed he had become obsessed with a chatbot on the platform. coreStoryFacts.text: The opposition to the Disney sale was led by a similar but not identical coalition of state AGs.
They fought against a proposed $20 million licensing deal that would give Disney access to Character.ai’s intellectual property, but not to users’ chats.
What happens to your private conversations when an AI company goes bankrupt ?
Only one anonymous bidder for the chat data has been disclosed so far: Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC (Smirks), which was set up as a Delaware company on November 13, 2026.
The following day, Character.ai picked it as the base bid for the auction, scheduled for December 1, California Attorney General Rob Bonta noted .
It is unclear what the buyer’s plans are for the chats.
Now they want to abuse the bankruptcy process to do exactly what they said they wouldn’t do — auction off those private chat records and personal details to a shady buyer.”
In addition, the sale would involve other personal data, like IP addresses, the statements said.
The company also faced lawsuits related to child safety — one involved the suicide of a 14-year-old Florida boy whose mother claimed he had become obsessed with a chatbot on the platform.
“Character.AI promised consumers that their data would not be sold.
This kind of behavior is illegal under federal and California law and bankruptcy should not be used to sidestep these consumer protections,” Bonta said in a statement.

extraction.body: What happens to your private conversations when an AI company goes bankrupt ? If it’s Character.ai, apparently, the plan is to auction them off to the highest bidder. Now, a coalition of 42 state attorneys general is intervening in Character.ai’s bankruptcy proceedings in an effort to stop the chatbot maker from selling off sensitive user data, which includes the private conversations of millions of users. The attorneys general involved in the matter have put out individual press releases , claiming that Character.ai’s dataset includes chat histories from more than 21 million U.S. accounts, more than 2.1 million of which belong to minors. In addition, the sale would involve other personal data, like IP addresses, the statements said. Only one anonymous bidder for the chat data has been disclosed so far: Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC (Smirks), which was set up as a Delaware company on November 13, 2026. The following day, Character.ai picked it as the base bid for the auction, scheduled for December 1, California Attorney General Rob Bonta noted . It is unclear what the buyer’s plans are for the chats. In addition, some states, including California, Colorado, New York, and Connecticut, have enacted chatbot safety legislation that will go into effect on January 1, 2027, which could trigger further violations if the sale goes through. “Character.AI promised consumers that their data would not be sold. This kind of behavior is illegal under federal and California law and bankruptcy should not be used to sidestep these consumer protections,” Bonta said in a statement. Connecticut Attorney General William Tong also criticized Character.ai’s business model. “Their chatbots drove vulnerable youth down a rabbit hole of emotionally volatile and sexually inappropriate chats,” Tong said . “Their reckless misconduct and broken business model drove their company into the ground. Now they want to abuse the bankruptcy process to do exactly what they said they wouldn’t do — auction off those private chat records and personal details to a shady buyer.” Tong added: “We objected to the Disney sale, and we’re calling on the bankruptcy court to reject this sale too as yet another guise to eviscerate legal liability and consumer protection.” The opposition to the Disney sale was led by a similar but not identical coalition of state AGs. They fought against a proposed $20 million licensing deal that would give Disney access to Character.ai’s intellectual property, but not to users’ chats. The deal has not yet received final court approval. (Disney also agreed to hire most of Character.ai’s remaining staff .) Character.ai suffered after its co-founders, Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, returned to Google , when the tech giant signed a non-exclusive license to use the AI startup’s tech. The company also faced lawsuits related to child safety — one involved the suicide of a 14-year-old Florida boy whose mother claimed he had become obsessed with a chatbot on the platform. Now, a coalition of 42 state attorneys general is intervening in Character.ai’s bankruptcy proceedings in an effort to stop the chatbot maker from selling off sensitive user data, which includes the private conversations of millions of users.

The attorneys general involved in the matter have put out individual press releases , claiming that Character.ai’s dataset includes chat histories from more than 21 million U.S. accounts, more than 2.1 million of which belong to minors. In addition, the sale would involve other personal data, like IP addresses, the statements said.

Only one anonymous bidder for the chat data has been disclosed so far: Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC (Smirks), which was set up as a Delaware company on November 13, 2026. The following day, Character.ai picked it as the base bid for the auction, scheduled for December 1, California Attorney General Rob Bonta noted . It is unclear what the buyer’s plans are for the chats.

In addition, some states, including California, Colorado, New York, and Connecticut, have enacted chatbot safety legislation that will go into effect on January 1, 2027, which could trigger further violations if the sale goes through.

“Character.AI promised consumers that their data would not be sold. This kind of behavior is illegal under federal and California law and bankruptcy should not be used to sidestep these consumer protections,” Bonta said in a statement.
Connecticut Attorney General William Tong also criticized Character.ai’s business model.

“Their chatbots drove vulnerable youth down a rabbit hole of emotionally volatile and sexually inappropriate chats,” Tong said . “Their reckless misconduct and broken business model drove their company into the ground. Now they want to abuse the bankruptcy process to do exactly what they said they wouldn’t do — auction off those private chat records and personal details to a shady buyer.”
Tong added: “We objected to the Disney sale, and we’re calling on the bankruptcy court to reject this sale too as yet another guise to eviscerate legal liability and consumer protection.”

The opposition to the Disney sale was led by a similar but not identical coalition of state AGs. They fought against a proposed $20 million licensing deal that would give Disney access to Character.ai’s intellectual property, but not to users’ chats. The deal has not yet received final court approval. (Disney also agreed to hire most of Character.ai’s remaining staff .)

Character.ai suffered after its co-founders, Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, returned to Google , when the tech giant signed a non-exclusive license to use the AI startup’s tech. The company also faced lawsuits related to child safety — one involved the suicide of a 14-year-old Florida boy whose mother claimed he had become obsessed with a chatbot on the platform.

California AG Bonta is joined in the effort to oppose the sale of Character.ai user data by attorneys general from Alaska, Arkansas, Colorado, Connecticut, the District of Columbia, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Missouri, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Utah, Virginia, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin, and West Virginia.

State attorneys general are asking a bankruptcy court to reject Character.AI’s proposed sale terms before its December 1, 2026 auction. According to the states, the deal would transfer private conversations and personal information covering more than 21 million U.S. accounts, including more than 2.1 million registered to minors , without binding protections for how a buyer uses that data. The coalition’s November 20 filing also asks the court to exclude certain sensitive data and models trained on it . The objection therefore reaches beyond access to stored conversations to assets developed using them. Oregon’s Department of Justice says the records include conversations about self-harm, eating disorders and suicidal thoughts, including exchanges with characters posing as therapists and physicians. The chats are linked to user profiles, IP addresses, location information and risk scores assigned by Character.AI . The states contrast those terms with Character.AI’s privacy-policy assurance: “we do not sell personal information for monetary consideration.” They also question the opening bidder, Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC, which they say was formed one day before its November 14 selection. Its contract names neither a parent company nor investors. The coalition wants the bidder rejected and its proposed $350,000 break-up fee denied. People poured their most private moments into this app, including kids who talked about self-harm and suicide and kids who were pulled into sexual conversations. Character.AI’s training disclosure says it uses user interactions to train models and that processed data may contain personal information. Kentucky’s attorney general alleges the company failed to obtain verifiable parental consent for children under 13 and used minors’ personal and emotional disclosures to improve its models. The states cite Federal Trade Commission precedents involving WW International, Kurbo and Everalbum. Those orders required destruction of specified data and models or algorithms built using it, Tech Policy Press explains — not just deletion of the underlying records . The court has ordered an independent consumer privacy ombudsman to examine proposed transfers involving accounts, chats, sensitive information and AI-related assets. Minnesota’s attorney general says the reviewer will identify privacy issues and propose protections before assets can be sold.
