extraction.body: Two Dutch groups asked the Amsterdam District Court on November 26, 2026, to halt sales of Meta smart glasses in the Netherlands. According to Reuters , Consumentenbond and Offlimits argue that the AI-powered glasses let wearers record people without their knowledge, which could break European privacy law. The case names Meta and EssilorLuxottica, the owner of Ray-Ban, as defendants. The filing goes beyond a simple sales stop. The plaintiffs also want the court to order Meta to prevent recording of people without their knowledge and to stop using such recordings to train AI models. Any ruling would apply only to the Netherlands, though Reuters reported that it could set a wider precedent for how camera-equipped eyewear is sold across Europe. This is the second Meta regulatory story on our desk this week. Days earlier we covered how Meta declined a UK FCA sandbox test and an ICO scheme for its Muse product, and the Dutch case adds a court fight on a separate continent and a separate product line. Below we lay out what is confirmed, what is not, and what it means for hardware buyers and makers. Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. The core request is blunt. Consumentenbond and Offlimits want the Amsterdam District Court to stop Meta and EssilorLuxottica from selling Meta smart glasses to Dutch consumers. That would pull a mainstream consumer wearable off the shelves in one EU country, which is a rare ask for any court in the hardware space. Reuters reported two additional measures. First, the plaintiffs want Meta ordered to build in protection against filming people who do not know they are being recorded. Second, they want the company to stop feeding recordings into the training of its AI models. Each of those asks would force a product change even if the court never orders a full sales halt. The reports do not say how the court will schedule the case, when a hearing will take place, or whether it will rule on the sales halt before it decides the broader privacy questions. We will not guess at a timetable. What we can say is that the request landed on the same day it was reported, so the case sits at the very start of its life. The plaintiffs are two separate Dutch organizations, Consumentenbond and Offlimits. Reuters named both. The fact sheet we work from does not describe their membership, funding, or past cases, so we will not pad this section with background we cannot verify. Two groups filing together does signal a coordinated effort rather than a one-off complaint. Notice what the plaintiffs did not ask for. Based on the reporting, they did not request damages in a figure we can quote, and no source we have identifies a dollar or euro amount. We also have no named spokesperson quote from either group in the material available to us, so this article paraphrases the filing as Reuters described it. Naming both companies matters. Meta builds the AI features and the software behind the glasses. EssilorLuxottica, which Reuters identified as the owner of Ray-Ban, brings the eyewear brand and the retail relationships. A court order aimed at only one of them could leave the other free to keep selling, so the plaintiffs chose to name both. That structure mirrors how the product reaches shoppers. A buyer walks into an optician or opens a retail page, sees a familiar frame brand, and gets a device that happens to carry a camera and an AI assistant. The legal question of who bears responsibility for bystander privacy sits across that whole chain, from software design to the shop counter. The plaintiffs frame the harm as covert recording. A phone raised toward a stranger signals intent, since everyone nearby can see the lens. A pair of glasses hides that signal. If the wearer films a conversation, a commute, or a child at a playground, the people in frame may never learn it happened. Reuters reported that the groups see this as a potential violation of European privacy laws. We cannot name the specific articles or statutes they cite, because the fact sheet does not list them. What we can say is that European privacy rules generally give people a say over how images of them are captured and used, and that is the territory the plaintiffs are stepping into. Privacy in shared spaces is a live design problem across hardware, not only for glasses. Even display makers now sell features aimed at shoulder-surfing, as our piece on Omdia’s forecast for active privacy view OLEDs showed. The Dutch case pushes the same instinct outward, from protecting your own screen to protecting strangers from your lens. Three traits set glasses apart in this argument. They sit at eye level, so they capture what the wearer looks at. They stay on for hours, so recording can start with a tap or a voice command. And they look like regular frames, so nearby people get no warning. None of those traits proves wrongdoing, but together they explain why regulators and consumer groups keep returning to this product category. The request to stop using recordings to train AI models may matter more to Meta’s business than the sales halt itself. A sales ban in one country of the EU is a bounded loss. A ban on training with recordings captured by the glasses touches how the company improves its assistant and its vision features worldwide. The reports do not detail what data Meta collects from the glasses or what share of it flows into training. We do not have those numbers, and we will not estimate them. The plaintiffs’ concern is clear enough without figures: people who never agreed to be filmed could end up as training material for a commercial model. The court filing did not arrive in a vacuum. On November 19, 2026, the Dutch privacy regulator, the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (AP), advised consumers not to buy smart glasses or AI-powered glasses with cameras. The agency reached that view after examining six types available on the Dutch market. That is seven days before the court request. A regulator telling the public to hold off on a whole product category is a strong signal, and it gives the plaintiffs a useful backdrop. The AP’s advice covers six types of glasses, so it is not limited to Meta’s product. We cannot say which six models the agency tested, since the fact sheet lists none. It is important to separate the two actions. The AP issued advice to consumers. Consumentenbond and Offlimits asked a court for an order against two companies. An advisory carries no legal force to stop a sale, while a court order could. The first action shapes public opinion, and the second tries to change what shops can legally sell. The most important line in that table is the court decision. As of today the case is a request, not a ruling. Headlines that suggest Meta glasses are already banned in the Netherlands overstate what the reporting supports. Reuters stressed that any ruling would apply to the Netherlands. In practical terms, a win for the plaintiffs would mean Meta and EssilorLuxottica could no longer sell the glasses to Dutch shoppers, or would have to change the product or its settings to meet the court’s conditions. Buyers in Belgium, Germany, or France would see no direct change. Even so, a national order in an EU country carries weight beyond its borders. Privacy law in Europe shares a common foundation, and lawyers and regulators in neighboring states watch each other’s cases. Reuters reported that the outcome could set a broader precedent, which is why a single-country dispute draws attention from companies that sell camera wearables across the bloc. A loss for the plaintiffs would matter too. If the court declines to act, Meta and EssilorLuxottica can point to the decision when they defend the product elsewhere. Either result will get quoted in future filings. That makes the Amsterdam case a test of whether civil courts, and not only regulators, will police consumer wearables. Wearable sensing is spreading well beyond the face. Researchers at ETH Zurich recently showed a sensor on a single tooth for silent speech, which we covered in our report on the InvisiSpeech tooth sensor . Devices that capture speech, images, or both without drawing attention keep multiplying, so the legal answers reached for glasses may end up shaping rules for many other gadgets. The AP reviewed six types of camera glasses, and the plaintiffs targeted Meta’s. That tells us the privacy question applies to the category, even if one company sits at the top of the complaint. Rivals building camera or audio wearables will read the Amsterdam filing closely, because the same arguments could be pointed at them. Audio recorders raise the sibling issue. When we looked at the Nothing Ear (note) and its four rivals , consent for the people being recorded was the central unresolved question there as well. A voice recorder in an earbud and a camera in a frame share one weakness: the person being captured often has no idea. The table below lays out who holds which position in the Dutch case, based only on the confirmed reporting. It shows how the views line up and where the open questions sit. The Netherlands is one market among many, so a sales halt there would not dent Meta’s global numbers in any way we can measure. We have no Dutch sales figures for the glasses, and we will not invent them. The risk sits elsewhere. A court order, or even a prolonged case, makes retailers nervous about stocking a product that a regulator told people not to buy. Opticians and electronics shops carry the exposure first. A store that sells the glasses may field questions from customers who read the AP advice. Some shops may pause promotion while the case runs. Others will keep selling and wait for a ruling. Without a court decision, each retailer must weigh reputational risk on its own. Meta’s relationship with European regulators already looks tense on other fronts, as the story of Meta flagging its own AI agent and then facing a $75,000 suit showed. A string of disputes does not prove a pattern, yet it raises the stakes for how the company handles the Dutch filing. The takeaway: two Dutch groups have asked a court to halt sales of Meta smart glasses over covert recording and AI training, and the court has not yet decided. The plaintiffs, the defendants, the regulator’s November 19 advice, and the Netherlands-only scope are all confirmed. The model, price, specifications, and any ruling are not. For readers, the useful move is to watch two things. One is whether the court agrees to hear the sales halt quickly. The other is whether Meta or EssilorLuxottica announces product changes in response. Either signal would show how seriously the companies take the privacy argument and how far the Amsterdam case could travel. Consumentenbond and Offlimits filed the request at the Amsterdam District Court, according to Reuters. The defendants are Meta and EssilorLuxottica, which Reuters identified as the owner of Ray-Ban. They want a halt to sales of Meta’s AI-powered smart glasses in the Netherlands. They also want the court to require Meta to prevent recording people without their knowledge and to stop using recordings to train AI models. No. Reporting so far describes a request, not a ruling. Nothing available to us shows that the court has granted a sales halt.

Two groups filing together does signal a coordinated effort rather than a one-off complaint.

Notice what the plaintiffs did not ask for. Based on the reporting, they did not request damages in a figure we can quote, and no source we have identifies a dollar or euro amount. We also have no named spokesperson quote from either group in the material available to us, so this article paraphrases the filing as Reuters described it.

Naming both companies matters. Meta builds the AI features and the software behind the glasses. EssilorLuxottica, which Reuters identified as the owner of Ray-Ban, brings the eyewear brand and the retail relationships. A court order aimed at only one of them could leave the other free to keep selling, so the plaintiffs chose to name both.

That structure mirrors how the product reaches shoppers. A buyer walks into an optician or opens a retail page, sees a familiar frame brand, and gets a device that happens to carry a camera and an AI assistant. The legal question of who bears responsibility for bystander privacy sits across that whole chain, from software design to the shop counter.

The plaintiffs frame the harm as covert recording. A phone raised toward a stranger signals intent, since everyone nearby can see the lens. A pair of glasses hides that signal. If the wearer films a conversation, a commute, or a child at a playground, the people in frame may never learn it happened.

Reuters reported that the groups see this as a potential violation of European privacy laws. We cannot name the specific articles or statutes they cite, because the fact sheet does not list them. What we can say is that European privacy rules generally give people a say over how images of them are captured and used, and that is the territory the plaintiffs are stepping into.

Privacy in shared spaces is a live design problem across hardware, not only for glasses. Even display makers now sell features aimed at shoulder-surfing, as our piece on Omdia’s forecast for active privacy view OLEDs showed. The Dutch case pushes the same instinct outward, from protecting your own screen to protecting strangers from your lens.

Three traits set glasses apart in this argument. They sit at eye level, so they capture what the wearer looks at. They stay on for hours, so recording can start with a tap or a voice command. And they look like regular frames, so nearby people get no warning. None of those traits proves wrongdoing, but together they explain why regulators and consumer groups keep returning to this product category.

The request to stop using recordings to train AI models may matter more to Meta’s business than the sales halt itself. A sales ban in one country of the EU is a bounded loss. A ban on training with recordings captured by the glasses touches how the company improves its assistant and its vision features worldwide.

The reports do not detail what data Meta collects from the glasses or what share of it flows into training. We do not have those numbers, and we will not estimate them. The plaintiffs’ concern is clear enough without figures: people who never agreed to be filmed could end up as training material for a commercial model.

The court filing did not arrive in a vacuum. On November 19, 2026, the Dutch privacy regulator, the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (AP), advised consumers not to buy smart glasses or AI-powered glasses with cameras. The agency reached that view after examining six types available on the Dutch market.

That is seven days before the court request. A regulator telling the public to hold off on a whole product category is a strong signal, and it gives the plaintiffs a useful backdrop. The AP’s advice covers six types of glasses, so it is not limited to Meta’s product. We cannot say which six models the agency tested, since the fact sheet lists none.

It is important to separate the two actions. The AP issued advice to consumers. Consumentenbond and Offlimits asked a court for an order against two companies. An advisory carries no legal force to stop a sale, while a court order could. The first action shapes public opinion, and the second tries to change what shops can legally sell.

The most important line in that table is the court decision. As of today the case is a request, not a ruling. Headlines that suggest Meta glasses are already banned in the Netherlands overstate what the reporting supports.

Reuters stressed that any ruling would apply to the Netherlands. In practical terms, a win for the plaintiffs would mean Meta and EssilorLuxottica could no longer sell the glasses to Dutch shoppers, or would have to change the product or its settings to meet the court’s conditions. Buyers in Belgium, Germany, or France would see no direct change.

Even so, a national order in an EU country carries weight beyond its borders. Privacy law in Europe shares a common foundation, and lawyers and regulators in neighboring states watch each other’s cases. Reuters reported that the outcome could set a broader precedent, which is why a single-country dispute draws attention from companies that sell camera wearables across the bloc.

A loss for the plaintiffs would matter too. If the court declines to act, Meta and EssilorLuxottica can point to the decision when they defend the product elsewhere. Either result will get quoted in future filings. That makes the Amsterdam case a test of whether civil courts, and not only regulators, will police consumer wearables.

Wearable sensing is spreading well beyond the face. Researchers at ETH Zurich recently showed a sensor on a single tooth for silent speech, which we covered in our report on the InvisiSpeech tooth sensor . Devices that capture speech, images, or both without drawing attention keep multiplying, so the legal answers reached for glasses may end up shaping rules for many other gadgets.

The AP reviewed six types of camera glasses, and the plaintiffs targeted Meta’s. That tells us the privacy question applies to the category, even if one company sits at the top of the complaint. Rivals building camera or audio wearables will read the Amsterdam filing closely, because the same arguments could be pointed at them.

Audio recorders raise the sibling issue. When we looked at the Nothing Ear (note) and its four rivals , consent for the people being recorded was the central unresolved question there as well. A voice recorder in an earbud and a camera in a frame share one weakness: the person being captured often has no idea.
The table below lays out who holds which position in the Dutch case, based only on the confirmed reporting. It shows how the views line up and where the open questions sit.

The Netherlands is one market among many, so a sales halt there would not dent Meta’s global numbers in any way we can measure. We have no Dutch sales figures for the glasses, and we will not invent them. The risk sits elsewhere. A court order, or even a prolonged case, makes retailers nervous about stocking a product that a regulator told people not to buy.

Opticians and electronics shops carry the exposure first. A store that sells the glasses may field questions from customers who read the AP advice. Some shops may pause promotion while the case runs. Others will keep selling and wait for a ruling. Without a court decision, each retailer must weigh reputational risk on its own.

Meta’s relationship with European regulators already looks tense on other fronts, as the story of Meta flagging its own AI agent and then facing a $75,000 suit showed. A string of disputes does not prove a pattern, yet it raises the stakes for how the company handles the Dutch filing.

The takeaway: two Dutch groups have asked a court to halt sales of Meta smart glasses over covert recording and AI training, and the court has not yet decided. The plaintiffs, the defendants, the regulator’s November 19 advice, and the Netherlands-only scope are all confirmed. The model, price, specifications, and any ruling are not.

For readers, the useful move is to watch two things. One is whether the court agrees to hear the sales halt quickly. The other is whether Meta or EssilorLuxottica announces product changes in response. Either signal would show how seriously the companies take the privacy argument and how far the Amsterdam case could travel.
Consumentenbond and Offlimits filed the request at the Amsterdam District Court, according to Reuters. The defendants are Meta and EssilorLuxottica, which Reuters identified as the owner of Ray-Ban.

They want a halt to sales of Meta’s AI-powered smart glasses in the Netherlands. They also want the court to require Meta to prevent recording people without their knowledge and to stop using recordings to train AI models.
No. Reporting so far describes a request, not a ruling. Nothing available to us shows that the court has granted a sales halt.

extraction.body: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg's ambitious push to bring AI into everyday life is facing another challenge. The company's Ray-Ban smart glasses are now facing a legal battle in the Netherlands, where consumer rights and digital privacy groups want their sales stopped over concerns that the devices could allow people to secretly record others. The groups have approached an Amsterdam court, asking it to stop Meta and eyewear company EssilorLuxottica from selling the camera-equipped smart glasses in the country until stronger privacy protections are introduced. The complaint raises questions about how easily people can be recorded without their knowledge especially in public places. According to a Reuters report, the Dutch consumer organisation Consumentenbond and digital rights group Offlimits want Meta to prevent users from recording people without their consent. They have also demanded that the company stop using footage captured through the glasses to train its artificial intelligence models. The groups have reportedly asked the court to impose penalties of up to 100,000 euros per day if Meta fails to follow the proposed restrictions. The maximum penalty could reach 100 million euros. The biggest concern is that these glasses look like regular eyewear but come with built-in cameras and microphones. This means someone can capture photographs or videos of people without making it immediately obvious that they are being recorded. The Zuckerberg-owned company, however, has rejected the allegations. The US-based social media giant has maintained that its smart glasses come with a recording indicator light that alerts people when someone is taking photographs or recording videos. EssilorLuxottica has also opposed the proposed restrictions, calling a sales ban disproportionate. This is not the first time Meta's smart glasses have faced privacy-related criticism. Earlier, a Dutch privacy watchdog advised consumers against buying camera-equipped smart glasses after identifying concerns involving covert recording, AI-generated advice and data security. The Amsterdam court is expected to deliver its decision in mid-December. (With inputs from Reuters)

passages: Dutch consumer protection and digital rights organizations have approached a court in Amsterdam seeking to stop the sale of Meta Platforms’ META smart glasses in the Netherlands, citing concerns over unauthorized recording and alleged breaches of European privacy regulations, Reuters reported on Thursday.
The legal challenge follows growing international scrutiny of the devices.
The Dutch privacy regulator recently advised consumers against purchasing them, while Germany's national consumer federation has initiated separate legal proceedings.
EssilorLuxottica ESLOF , Meta’s META manufacturing partner and Ray-Ban owner, told the court it has no access to the recorded footage.

Its legal team also rejected claims that recordings made in Europe are processed or used to train AI systems, citing the indicator light on the glasses as a notification that recording is taking place.

The case names Meta and EssilorLuxottica, the owner of Ray-Ban, as defendants. The filing goes beyond a simple sales stop. The plaintiffs also want the court to order Meta to prevent recording of people without their knowledge and to stop using such recordings to train AI models. Any ruling would apply only to the Netherlands, though Reuters reported that it could set a wider precedent for how camera-equipped eyewear is sold across Europe. This is the second Meta regulatory story on our desk this week. Days earlier we covered how Meta declined a UK FCA sandbox test and an ICO scheme for its Muse product, and the Dutch case adds a court fight on a separate continent and a separate product line. Below we lay out what is confirmed, what is not, and what it means for hardware buyers and makers. Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. The core request is blunt. Consumentenbond and Offlimits want the Amsterdam District Court to stop Meta and EssilorLuxottica from selling Meta smart glasses to Dutch consumers. That would pull a mainstream consumer wearable off the shelves in one EU country, which is a rare ask for any court in the hardware space. Reuters reported two additional measures. First, the plaintiffs want Meta ordered to build in protection against filming people who do not know they are being recorded. Second, they want the company to stop feeding recordings into the training of its AI models. Each of those asks would force a product change even if the court never orders a full sales halt. The reports do not say how the court will schedule the case, when a hearing will take place, or whether it will rule on the sales halt before it decides the broader privacy questions. We will not guess at a timetable. What we can say is that the request landed on the same day it was reported, so the case sits at the very start of its life. The plaintiffs are two separate Dutch organizations, Consumentenbond and Offlimits. Reuters named both. The fact sheet we work from does not describe their membership, funding, or past cases, so we will not pad this section with background we cannot verify. Two groups filing together does signal a coordinated effort rather than a one-off complaint. Notice what the plaintiffs did not ask for. Based on the reporting, they did not request damages in a figure we can quote, and no source we have identifies a dollar or euro amount. We also have no named spokesperson quote from either group in the material available to us, so this article paraphrases the filing as Reuters described it. Naming both companies matters. Meta builds the AI features and the software behind the glasses. EssilorLuxottica, which Reuters identified as the owner of Ray-Ban, brings the eyewear brand and the retail relationships. A court order aimed at only one of them could leave the other free to keep selling, so the plaintiffs chose to name both. That structure mirrors how the product reaches shoppers. A buyer walks into an optician or opens a retail page, sees a familiar frame brand, and gets a device that happens to carry a camera and an AI assistant. The legal question of who bears responsibility for bystander privacy sits across that whole chain, from software design to the shop counter. The plaintiffs frame the harm as covert recording. A phone raised toward a stranger signals intent, since everyone nearby can see the lens. A pair of glasses hides that signal. If the wearer films a conversation, a commute, or a child at a playground, the people in frame may never learn it happened. Reuters reported that the groups see this as a potential violation of European privacy laws. We cannot name the specific articles or statutes they cite, because the fact sheet does not list them. What we can say is that European privacy rules generally give people a say over how images of them are captured and used, and that is the territory the plaintiffs are stepping into. Privacy in shared spaces is a live design problem across hardware, not only for glasses. Even display makers now sell features aimed at shoulder-surfing, as our piece on Omdia’s forecast for active privacy view OLEDs showed. The Dutch case pushes the same instinct outward, from protecting your own screen to protecting strangers from your lens. Three traits set glasses apart in this argument. They sit at eye level, so they capture what the wearer looks at. They stay on for hours, so recording can start with a tap or a voice command. And they look like regular frames, so nearby people get no warning. None of those traits proves wrongdoing, but together they explain why regulators and consumer groups keep returning to this product category. The request to stop using recordings to train AI models may matter more to Meta’s business than the sales halt itself. A sales ban in one country of the EU is a bounded loss. A ban on training with recordings captured by the glasses touches how the company improves its assistant and its vision features worldwide. The reports do not detail what data Meta collects from the glasses or what share of it flows into training. We do not have those numbers, and we will not estimate them. The plaintiffs’ concern is clear enough without figures: people who never agreed to be filmed could end up as training material for a commercial model. The court filing did not arrive in a vacuum. On November 19, 2026, the Dutch privacy regulator, the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (AP), advised consumers not to buy smart glasses or AI-powered glasses with cameras. The agency reached that view after examining six types available on the Dutch market. That is seven days before the court request. A regulator telling the public to hold off on a whole product category is a strong signal, and it gives the plaintiffs a useful backdrop. An advisory carries no legal force to stop a sale, while a court order could. The first action shapes public opinion, and the second tries to change what shops can legally sell. The most important line in that table is the court decision. As of today the case is a request, not a ruling. In practical terms, a win for the plaintiffs would mean Meta and EssilorLuxottica could no longer sell the glasses to Dutch shoppers, or would have to change the product or its settings to meet the court’s conditions. Buyers in Belgium, Germany, or France would see no direct change. Even so, a national order in an EU country carries weight beyond its borders. Privacy law in Europe shares a common foundation, and lawyers and regulators in neighboring states watch each other’s cases. Reuters reported that the outcome could set a broader precedent, which is why a single-country dispute draws attention from companies that sell camera wearables across the bloc. A loss for the plaintiffs would matter too. If the court declines to act, Meta and EssilorLuxottica can point to the decision when they defend the product elsewhere. Either result will get quoted in future filings. That makes the Amsterdam case a test of whether civil courts, and not only regulators, will police consumer wearables. Wearable sensing is spreading well beyond the face. Researchers at ETH Zurich recently showed a sensor on a single tooth for silent speech, which we covered in our report on the InvisiSpeech tooth sensor . Devices that capture speech, images, or both without drawing attention keep multiplying, so the legal answers reached for glasses may end up shaping rules for many other gadgets. The AP reviewed six types of camera glasses, and the plaintiffs targeted Meta’s. That tells us the privacy question applies to the category, even if one company sits at the top of the complaint. Rivals building camera or audio wearables will read the Amsterdam filing closely, because the same arguments could be pointed at them. Audio recorders raise the sibling issue. When we looked at the Nothing Ear (note) and its four rivals , consent for the people being recorded was the central unresolved question there as well. A voice recorder in an earbud and a camera in a frame share one weakness: the person being captured often has no idea. The table below lays out who holds which position in the Dutch case, based only on the confirmed reporting. It shows how the views line up and where the open questions sit. The Netherlands is one market among many, so a sales halt there would not dent Meta’s global numbers in any way we can measure. We have no Dutch sales figures for the glasses, and we will not invent them. The risk sits elsewhere. A court order, or even a prolonged case, makes retailers nervous about stocking a product that a regulator told people not to buy. Opticians and electronics shops carry the exposure first. A store that sells the glasses may field questions from customers who read the AP advice. Some shops may pause promotion while the case runs. Others will keep selling and wait for a ruling. Without a court decision, each retailer must weigh reputational risk on its own. Meta’s relationship with European regulators already looks tense on other fronts, as the story of Meta flagging its own AI agent and then facing a $75,000 suit showed. A string of disputes does not prove a pattern, yet it raises the stakes for how the company handles the Dutch filing. The takeaway: two Dutch groups have asked a court to halt sales of Meta smart glasses over covert recording and AI training, and the court has not yet decided. The plaintiffs, the defendants, the regulator’s November 19 advice, and the Netherlands-only scope are all confirmed. The model, price, specifications, and any ruling are not. For readers, the useful move is to watch two things. One is whether the court agrees to hear the sales halt quickly. The other is whether Meta or EssilorLuxottica announces product changes in response. Either signal would show how seriously the companies take the privacy argument and how far the Amsterdam case could travel. They also want the court to require Meta to prevent recording people without their knowledge and to stop using recordings to train AI models. No. Reporting so far describes a request, not a ruling. The company's Ray-Ban smart glasses are now facing a legal battle in the Netherlands, where consumer rights and digital privacy groups want their sales stopped over concerns that the devices could allow people to secretly record others. The groups have approached an Amsterdam court, asking it to stop Meta and eyewear company EssilorLuxottica from selling the camera-equipped smart glasses in the country until stronger privacy protections are introduced. The complaint raises questions about how easily people can be recorded without their knowledge especially in public places. According to a Reuters report, the Dutch consumer organisation Consumentenbond and digital rights group Offlimits want Meta to prevent users from recording people without their consent. They have also demanded that the company stop using footage captured through the glasses to train its artificial intelligence models. The groups have reportedly asked the court to impose penalties of up to 100,000 euros per day if Meta fails to follow the proposed restrictions. The maximum penalty could reach 100 million euros. The biggest concern is that these glasses look like regular eyewear but come with built-in cameras and microphones. This means someone can capture photographs or videos of people without making it immediately obvious that they are being recorded. The Zuckerberg-owned company, however, has rejected the allegations. The US-based social media giant has maintained that its smart glasses come with a recording indicator light that alerts people when someone is taking photographs or recording videos. EssilorLuxottica has also opposed the proposed restrictions, calling a sales ban disproportionate. This is not the first time Meta's smart glasses have faced privacy-related criticism. Earlier, a Dutch privacy watchdog advised consumers against buying camera-equipped smart glasses after identifying concerns involving covert recording, AI-generated advice and data security. The Amsterdam court is expected to deliver its decision in mid-December. (With inputs from Reuters)

The legal challenge follows growing international scrutiny of the devices.
The Dutch privacy regulator recently advised consumers against purchasing them, while Germany's national consumer federation has initiated separate legal proceedings.
EssilorLuxottica ESLOF , Meta’s META manufacturing partner and Ray-Ban owner, told the court it has no access to the recorded footage.

Its legal team also rejected claims that recordings made in Europe are processed or used to train AI systems, citing the indicator light on the glasses as a notification that recording is taking place.

extraction.body: Dutch consumer protection and digital rights organizations have approached a court in Amsterdam seeking to stop the sale of Meta Platforms’ META smart glasses in the Netherlands, citing concerns over unauthorized recording and alleged breaches of European privacy regulations, Reuters reported on Thursday. The action, brought by Consumentenbond and Offlimits, seeks restrictions on the use of footage captured through the devices, including a ban on using such recordings to develop AI models. The groups have also asked the court to suspend sales until the alleged violations are addressed. They are seeking financial penalties of up to €100,000 per day for each defendant, subject to a combined cap of €100 million. Meta META has challenged the demands, arguing that product manufacturers should not be held accountable for intentional misuse by individual users. Its legal team also rejected claims that recordings made in Europe are processed or used to train AI systems, citing the indicator light on the glasses as a notification that recording is taking place. EssilorLuxottica ESLOF , Meta’s META manufacturing partner and Ray-Ban owner, told the court it has no access to the recorded footage. The legal challenge follows growing international scrutiny of the devices. The Dutch privacy regulator recently advised consumers against purchasing them, while Germany's national consumer federation has initiated separate legal proceedings. LONDON - Standard Chartered’s crypto custody subsidiary Zodia Custody said it had suffered a security breach, exposing some client and staff information. An unauthorised party who breached its platform was able to access “limited client information, consisting of publicly available organisation details and, for a small number of clients and employees, a business contact name and e-mail address,” Zodia Custody chief executive officer Richard Clark said in a statement. The company had detected attempts to break into its platform on Nov 23 and took action, including turning off some of its software and applying additional security measures, Clark said. “We have contacted our clients and informed the relevant regulatory authorities,” Clark added. “Based on our investigation to date, there have been no unauthorised transactions.” Standard Chartered merged the crypto custody business of Zodia with its own operations in an acquisition deal in early 2026 , having previously been the unit’s majority shareholder. extraction.body: Help Net Security newsletters : Daily and weekly news, cybersecurity jobs, open source projects, breaking news – subscribe here! An attacker who got into a 1Password employee’s corporate GitHub account went on to copy account records for some of the company’s users and source code from private repositories, the password manager maker disclosed on Wednesday. “1Password identified a security incident involving some of our backend systems,” the company wrote in a post it plans to keep updated. “On November 19, 2026, 1Password began investigating indications that an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. The actor used the account to access source code and push malicious code to backend services, which downloaded administrative data pertaining to our customers,” the company detailed. The post doesn’t explain how the employee’s access was obtained, and it gives no date for when the intruder was detected or shut out. “At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker,” 1Password stated. The keys that protect vaults and the account recovery keys weren’t reached either, with the company reporting that its apps, browser extensions and services kept working normally. “1Password does not have access to your password or secret keys,” it added. The records pulled down by the malicious code belong to “a subset of our users,” and 1Password hasn’t said how many people that covers or whether individual, business or family accounts were affected. Each record holds the name and email address a customer uses with 1Password, account and user identifiers, the date the account was created and the time of its last sign-in. The attacker also got the public keys tied to those accounts, which are “public by design” and have “no impact to user security,” the company noted. Secure Remote Password (SRP) protocol parameters were taken too, and 1Password maintains these “cannot be used to access your account.” Another part of the haul affects a smaller group. Tokens from invitation, provisioning and account recovery emails were copied, though a token only works “when combined with an SSO sign-in or a six digit code.” 1Password has since lengthened the code from six digits to ten alphanumeric characters and contacted the small number of users affected. So far, the company has “validated no internal evidence of user account takeovers or compromise using any exposed account provisioning tokens.” The rest was internal metadata, “version numeric identifiers” and “file numeric identifiers” tied to its internal architecture, which the company lists as non-secret. The attacker also got into the company’s CI/CD system. “Our source code is not customer data, and contains no user secrets,” 1Password noted. Infrastructure secrets kept in CI/CD have been rotated. The compromised GitHub account was disabled, the token the attacker stole revoked and the access the attacker had set up removed. Internal credentials that may have leaked were rotated or revoked. On top of that, 1Password said it has tightened its GitHub, CI/CD and endpoint controls, added new detections, and brought in independent cybersecurity experts to validate the cleanup. passages: This article was originally published as Switzerland Approves Crypto Tax Data Sharing With 57 Jurisdictions on Crypto Breaking News – your trusted source for crypto news, Bitcoin news, and blockchain updates.
Switzerland’s Federal Council has approved 57 potential partner jurisdictions for the automatic exchange of information related to crypto assets, with the process set to begin in 2028.
The decision is designed to broaden how far Swiss tax authorities can reach across borders when investigating taxpayers’ crypto activity.

Switzerland’s original plan contemplated implementing crypto tax information requirements in 2026, but lawmakers had not finalized which counterpart jurisdictions would be involved—an uncertainty that contributed to a delay of at least one year, according to earlier reporting from Cointelegraph .
For readers, the key point is that Switzerland’s 57-jurisdiction approval doesn’t operate in isolation.

It increases the number of places where Swiss tax data could potentially be reflected or acted upon—depending on each jurisdiction’s willingness to participate and its ability to meet the standards for confidentiality and data security.

For investors and businesses operating in multiple countries, the practical impact of Switzerland’s approval is straightforward: more jurisdictions become potential receivers of crypto-related tax data.
Switzerland has already built a foundation for automatic information exchange of financial account data.

That continuity matters for taxpayers and service providers because it suggests Switzerland intends to integrate crypto reporting into a broader transparency architecture rather than treating it as a one-off initiative.

extraction.body: Switzerland’s Federal Council has approved 57 potential partner jurisdictions for the automatic exchange of information related to crypto assets, with the process set to begin in 2028. The decision is designed to broaden how far Swiss tax authorities can reach across borders when investigating taxpayers’ crypto activity. In a Wednesday announcement , the government said the list includes all European Union member states, the United Kingdom, and several G20 countries. Switzerland will only exchange information with jurisdictions that indicate interest and can comply with international confidentiality and data-security standards. For investors and businesses operating in multiple countries, the practical impact of Switzerland’s approval is straightforward: more jurisdictions become potential receivers of crypto-related tax data. Instead of relying solely on bilateral requests or limited domestic reporting regimes, authorities can use an automatic process to cross-check identities, residency, and transaction details tied to covered crypto activities. The Federal Council’s decision also helps remove a key bottleneck that previously affected timing. Switzerland’s original plan contemplated implementing crypto tax information requirements in 2026, but lawmakers had not finalized which counterpart jurisdictions would be involved—an uncertainty that contributed to a delay of at least one year, according to earlier reporting from Cointelegraph . Under the revised schedule, crypto service providers could begin collecting relevant data as early as Jan. 1, 2027. The first exchanges of information between tax authorities would then take place in 2028. The staggered structure is important for market participants. It means that compliance preparation is not just an “on day one” requirement; it starts before any information is actually shared internationally. For service providers captured by the rules, that translates into earlier work on data capture, recordkeeping, and processes to identify customers’ tax residency and relevant transactional activity. Switzerland’s approach also aligns with how broader information-exchange regimes are typically implemented: the reporting groundwork begins while partner jurisdictions finalize readiness and procedural standards. The reporting requirements fall under the OECD’s Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework (CARF). CARF is designed to reduce opportunities for tax evasion by requiring certain crypto exchanges and other covered intermediaries to report key details to tax authorities. Those details include customer identity information, tax residency, and transaction data. The framework’s stated purpose is to close gaps in tax enforcement that arise when crypto transactions can cross borders without corresponding transparency obligations. Switzerland’s State Secretariat for International Finance describes the CARF-based approach as a supplement to an existing transparency system for financial accounts. The government’s view is that the crypto reporting layer will address areas where current account information exchange may not fully capture crypto-related activity. Switzerland has already built a foundation for automatic information exchange of financial account data. According to the Swiss government, it introduced the legal framework for that system in 2017 and has since exchanged financial account information with 113 jurisdictions, with exchanges reported for 2026. By approving partner jurisdictions for CARF, Switzerland is effectively extending the same cross-border compliance logic to crypto assets. That continuity matters for taxpayers and service providers because it suggests Switzerland intends to integrate crypto reporting into a broader transparency architecture rather than treating it as a one-off initiative. The move also fits into the wider international rollout of CARF. The European Union introduced crypto reporting requirements under the OECD framework in January, with the first international exchanges scheduled for 2027. As of March, the European Commission said 76 jurisdictions worldwide had committed to exchanging information under CARF. For readers, the key point is that Switzerland’s 57-jurisdiction approval doesn’t operate in isolation. It increases the number of places where Swiss tax data could potentially be reflected or acted upon—depending on each jurisdiction’s willingness to participate and its ability to meet the standards for confidentiality and data security. Going forward, market participants should watch for the operational details that determine how compliance will work in practice—especially around what data crypto service providers must collect starting in 2027, and which of the approved jurisdictions actively begin exchanges in 2028. Because Switzerland’s sharing is contingent on both interest and compliance with international safeguards, the effective scope of information exchange may evolve as jurisdictions confirm readiness. extraction.body: Switzerland’s Federal Council has approved 57 potential partner jurisdictions for the automatic exchange of information related to crypto assets, with the process set to begin in 2028. The decision is designed to broaden how far Swiss tax authorities can reach across borders when investigating taxpayers’ crypto activity. In a Wednesday announcement , the government said the list includes all European Union member states, the United Kingdom, and several G20 countries. Switzerland will only exchange information with jurisdictions that indicate interest and can comply with international confidentiality and data-security standards. For investors and businesses operating in multiple countries, the practical impact of Switzerland’s approval is straightforward: more jurisdictions become potential receivers of crypto-related tax data. Instead of relying solely on bilateral requests or limited domestic reporting regimes, authorities can use an automatic process to cross-check identities, residency, and transaction details tied to covered crypto activities. The Federal Council’s decision also helps remove a key bottleneck that previously affected timing. Switzerland’s original plan contemplated implementing crypto tax information requirements in 2026, but lawmakers had not finalized which counterpart jurisdictions would be involved—an uncertainty that contributed to a delay of at least one year, according to earlier reporting from Cointelegraph . Under the revised schedule, crypto service providers could begin collecting relevant data as early as Jan. 1, 2027. The first exchanges of information between tax authorities would then take place in 2028. The staggered structure is important for market participants. It means that compliance preparation is not just an “on day one” requirement; it starts before any information is actually shared internationally. For service providers captured by the rules, that translates into earlier work on data capture, recordkeeping, and processes to identify customers’ tax residency and relevant transactional activity. Switzerland’s approach also aligns with how broader information-exchange regimes are typically implemented: the reporting groundwork begins while partner jurisdictions finalize readiness and procedural standards. The reporting requirements fall under the OECD’s Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework (CARF). CARF is designed to reduce opportunities for tax evasion by requiring certain crypto exchanges and other covered intermediaries to report key details to tax authorities. Those details include customer identity information, tax residency, and transaction data. The framework’s stated purpose is to close gaps in tax enforcement that arise when crypto transactions can cross borders without corresponding transparency obligations. Switzerland’s State Secretariat for International Finance describes the CARF-based approach as a supplement to an existing transparency system for financial accounts. The government’s view is that the crypto reporting layer will address areas where current account information exchange may not fully capture crypto-related activity. Switzerland has already built a foundation for automatic information exchange of financial account data. According to the Swiss government, it introduced the legal framework for that system in 2017 and has since exchanged financial account information with 113 jurisdictions, with exchanges reported for 2026. By approving partner jurisdictions for CARF, Switzerland is effectively extending the same cross-border compliance logic to crypto assets. That continuity matters for taxpayers and service providers because it suggests Switzerland intends to integrate crypto reporting into a broader transparency architecture rather than treating it as a one-off initiative. The move also fits into the wider international rollout of CARF. The European Union introduced crypto reporting requirements under the OECD framework in January, with the first international exchanges scheduled for 2027. As of March, the European Commission said 76 jurisdictions worldwide had committed to exchanging information under CARF. For readers, the key point is that Switzerland’s 57-jurisdiction approval doesn’t operate in isolation. It increases the number of places where Swiss tax data could potentially be reflected or acted upon—depending on each jurisdiction’s willingness to participate and its ability to meet the standards for confidentiality and data security. Going forward, market participants should watch for the operational details that determine how compliance will work in practice—especially around what data crypto service providers must collect starting in 2027, and which of the approved jurisdictions actively begin exchanges in 2028. Because Switzerland’s sharing is contingent on both interest and compliance with international safeguards, the effective scope of information exchange may evolve as jurisdictions confirm readiness. extraction.body: Rising electricity demand is locking in fossil-fuel generation. In May 2025, my colleague David Rotman wrote a feature story describing how AI could keep us dependent on natural gas. Just 18 months later, I’ve lost count of how many times he’s already been proved right. Sure, it’s technically possible to meet the world’s rising electricity demand with other power sources, including renewables like wind and solar supported by batteries. But the reality in the US so far is that the data center boom is helping to fuel a massive natural-gas resurgence. Just one example: Plans for the Meta data center in Louisiana that David focused on in his story have expanded, and its power needs have too. The local utility went from three planned natural-gas plants to 10 . And as I wrote in a new story this week, data center developers are now looking beyond the grid and planning to build their own off-grid gas power plants . How did we get here? If you want to understand the future of the grid, one way to do it is by looking at interconnection queues—lists of power plants that have requested a connection to the system. In recent years these queues have been dominated by renewables like wind and solar power, which are generally the cheapest way to build new energy capacity today. But there’s been a shift in some places, particularly for PJM, the country’s largest power grid operator, which covers parts of 13 states in an area stretching from Illinois to Washington, DC. PJM has seen a major uptick in natural-gas proposals. In August, the operator announced that it had accepted proposals for 715 total projects with a capacity of over 200 gigawatts to join its queue. Nearly half that total capacity represented natural-gas plants. If all the projects in the queue were built, it would increase the fossil-fuel share on PJM’s grid from 61% to 67%, according to an analysis by Kevin Kircher , an energy modeler and assistant professor of mechanical engineering at Purdue. PJM’s queue is reflective of a bigger trend across the US. Natural gas is already the single biggest source of electricity in the country, and it has basically become the default to meet exploding power demand. This AI-driven rush is already affecting greenhouse-gas emissions for tech companies. Meta’s emissions are up 45% over last year’s, according to the company’s recently released 2026 Sustainability Report . That’s even higher than the jumps from fellow hyperscalers Google ( 18% ), Amazon ( 16% ), and Microsoft ( 25% ). The company is also “reevaluating” its 2030 goal to reach net-zero emissions, according to the report, though there aren’t details about how or when it might reach a decision there. And there’s another tidbit in that Meta report worth noting: The company said that when the grid can’t deliver power “on the necessary timeline,” it will look to other methods, including building its own on-site power generation. This fits into a related and growing trend that I’ve been tracking recently: Data center developers are looking to bypass long wait times to hook up to the grid by building their own power plants instead. It’s not new for large industrial facilities to supply their own power. Chemical plants often have natural-gas infrastructure on-site to generate electricity and heat, for example (though they’re generally connected to the grid as well). Mining operations are often remote, requiring an off-grid power source. But the desire to come online quickly means there could be a massive boom in off-grid power plants for data centers. Over 100 such facilities have been proposed in the US, with a total capacity of 115 gigawatts (that’s more than double the entire peak power demand of California). The vast majority of these sites have been proposed since the beginning of 2025. There are alternative ways to help meet growing electricity demand: Wind and solar are inexpensive options, and pairing them with batteries could improve their reliability, for example. I’ve also written before about demand flexibility —efforts to limit power drawn from the grid when demand is high. Right now, though, the evidence continues to stack up that the AI boom in the US is basically synonymous with a natural-gas boom. This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review ’s weekly climate newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Wednesday, sign up here .

sources.title: OpenAI says heavy ChatGPT users may hit limits sooner as it merges Chat and Work
passages: That’s among the concerns raised by some ChatGPT subscribers on social media and OpenAI’s community forum recently.

The users fear that merging the usage limits for Chat and Work could leave them with less access to advanced reasoning models than they currently have, even as they continue paying the same subscription fees .
Conversations using the Instant model will, however, remain unlimited and will not count toward the shared allowance.
Users can also continue using Instant after exhausting their usage limits.
The spokesperson added that OpenAI would continue working to improve efficiency so subscribers could get more out of their plans.
The ChatGPT maker began introducing the update to a small group of Pro subscribers, product lead Thibault “Tibo” Sottiaux said in a post on X on Tuesday.
An OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch that while most users are not expected to face more frequent usage resets, a small fraction of its heaviest users may hit their limits sooner.
Similar to OpenAI, rival Anthropic also moved to bring its conversational chat service Claude and work-focused Cowork under one interface in September.
Bringing conversational and work-related tools into a single interface could also make AI chatbots simpler to use, allowing users to move between chats and more complex tasks without switching tabs.

extraction.body: OpenAI has started rolling out a unified Chat and Work experience in ChatGPT to a few of its users, amid criticism from some subscribers that the merger could restrict their usage. The ChatGPT maker began introducing the update to a small group of Pro subscribers, product lead Thibault “Tibo” Sottiaux said in a post on X on Tuesday. The rollout follows OpenAI’s earlier announcement of the merger in an email to users. An OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch that while most users are not expected to face more frequent usage resets, a small fraction of its heaviest users may hit their limits sooner. That’s among the concerns raised by some ChatGPT subscribers on social media and OpenAI’s community forum recently. The users fear that merging the usage limits for Chat and Work could leave them with less access to advanced reasoning models than they currently have, even as they continue paying the same subscription fees . Under the new system, Chat and Work will share a single usage meter across ChatGPT, the OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch. Conversations using the Instant model will, however, remain unlimited and will not count toward the shared allowance. Users can also continue using Instant after exhausting their usage limits. The spokesperson added that OpenAI would continue working to improve efficiency so subscribers could get more out of their plans. While the rollout has started for a small group of users, OpenAI plans to bring shared usage limits more broadly in December, per its support page. Similar to OpenAI, rival Anthropic also moved to bring its conversational chat service Claude and work-focused Cowork under one interface in September. The changes come as AI companies face mounting infrastructure costs and growing demand for increasingly capable models, putting pressure on their computing resources. Bringing conversational and work-related tools into a single interface could also make AI chatbots simpler to use, allowing users to move between chats and more complex tasks without switching tabs. sources.title: Preinstalled Keenadu malware turns up on 220,000+ Android devices - Help Net Security
passages: Keenadu , one of the two families behind most of these infections, landed on more than 220,000 devices in the first ten months of 2026.
Together with the older Triada family, it turned up on 88% of devices found with preinstalled malware this year.
Triada was first discovered about ten years ago, and about twenty distinct variants of it appeared in 2026.
Help Net Security newsletters : Daily and weekly news, cybersecurity jobs, open source projects, breaking news – subscribe here!
Kaspersky believes the delay was meant to help the malware avoid detection.
Keenadu borrows this same modular design from Triada, letting attackers push extra modules onto a device and inject them into target apps.
In most known Keenadu attacks, the malware was used for ad fraud, in particular to generate fake clicks.

Most cases involve phones and tablets, though Kaspersky has found other preinstalled malware families in different hardware, with Dwphon in the firmware of children’s smartwatches and Vo1d in TV boxes.

Companies that issue these devices to staff can end up with slower phones, ads running on them, some visible to the user and some hidden, hijacked accounts, stolen cryptocurrency and leaked corporate data, the security firm noted.

“The latest Triada versions have two key distinguishing features: the ability to inject malicious functionality into any app on the device, system or user-installed, and a modular architecture that lets attackers tailor the malware to their current targets with additional payloads,” researchers explained.
Malware of this kind reaches a device through a supply chain attack.
Kaspersky advises companies to inspect and pilot-test sample units before ordering a large batch, while stressing that this step does not replace security software on each device.

A new Android phone can come out of the box with malware already in its firmware, and the number of such devices detected each month has grown more than 2.5 times over the past year, according to Kaspersky. Keenadu , one of the two families behind most of these infections, landed on more than 220,000 devices in the first ten months of 2026. Together with the older Triada family, it turned up on 88% of devices found with preinstalled malware this year. Triada was first discovered about ten years ago, and about twenty distinct variants of it appeared in 2026. “The latest Triada versions have two key distinguishing features: the ability to inject malicious functionality into any app on the device, system or user-installed, and a modular architecture that lets attackers tailor the malware to their current targets with additional payloads,” researchers explained. The Keenadu backdoor versions Kaspersky examined stayed silent for about two and a half months before their command-and-control servers sent the order to activate. Kaspersky believes the delay was meant to help the malware avoid detection. Keenadu borrows this same modular design from Triada, letting attackers push extra modules onto a device and inject them into target apps. In most known Keenadu attacks, the malware was used for ad fraud, in particular to generate fake clicks. Malware of this kind reaches a device through a supply chain attack. In some cases the manufacturer installs it on purpose. In others, a legitimate brand that assembles the final product receives malicious firmware from a contractor acting in bad faith, or a component used in the build process has been compromised. Once the malware is in the system partition, it is “technically impossible for either antivirus tools or the OS itself” to remove it, Kaspersky warned. Some of these Trojans are hard or impossible to get rid of even by reflashing the device. Most cases involve phones and tablets, though Kaspersky has found other preinstalled malware families in different hardware, with Dwphon in the firmware of children’s smartwatches and Vo1d in TV boxes. Companies that issue these devices to staff can end up with slower phones, ads running on them, some visible to the user and some hidden, hijacked accounts, stolen cryptocurrency and leaked corporate data, the security firm noted. Infected devices can be enlisted into proxy networks or DDoS botnets, and attackers who disable devices in daily use can disrupt a company’s operations. Kaspersky advises companies to inspect and pilot-test sample units before ordering a large batch, while stressing that this step does not replace security software on each device. “Even if the tests come out fine, an unscrupulous supplier may have deliberately sent clean units for inspection. Protection must also be continuous because, for example, the device update system could come under attack,” the researchers concluded .

extraction.body: Password manager maker 1Password has confirmed that some customer information was taken in a recent intrusion into its internal systems, but that customer password vaults and other secrets were not accessed. The Toronto-based tech company said in a blog post published Wednesday that it detected an intrusion on November 19, in which an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate account with GitHub, which the company uses to share and store its source code. The attacker used that employee’s access to push malicious code to the company’s internal servers, which allowed the hacker to download some data about 1Password customers, including their names and the email address that they use for logging into their account. The company said that the attacker also took details about when a 1Password account was created and when a user last logged in. 1Password said that customer vaults, which store their passwords, were “at no point” available to the attacker. The company also said that it doesn’t have access to customer account passwords or their secret keys, which are used to scramble their passwords so that 1Password cannot see them. In addition, the company said that its apps and extensions are unaffected by the incident. It’s unclear how the attacker gained access to the employee’s corporate account, and a spokesperson for 1Password did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s questions about the incident. 1Password did not say whether it had notified customers whose information was taken in the breach, or how many customers had information taken. We’ve also asked if the company has received any communication or demands from the hackers. We’ll update if we hear back from 1Password. The company touts millions of customers and more than 200,000 businesses who use its password manager products to store their passwords, credentials, payment card information, and more. Security experts have long recommended password managers as a better way of generating stronger credentials and keeping track of online accounts. sources.title: The next generation of bionic hands is here—and they can feel
passages: Davidson, now 33 and a trauma therapist, went on to have physical therapy and adjusted to life in his changed body.
The first one, which he received a year and a half after his injury, was a basic hook that allowed him to pick things up.
It wasn’t fancy, but it gave him “a psychological feeling of returning to being whole,” he says.
The hand is part of the bionic LUKE arm, named after Luke Skywalker of Star Wars , who was fitted with a lifelike prosthetic arm after his own was light-sabered off .
The arm was developed in the 2000s , initially trialed in 2014 , and approved by the FDA that same year.
The trial that Davidson is enrolled in isn’t so focused on the arm itself but on a new way to connect it to a person’s nervous system.
The connection allows users to control movements and receive feedback about how much pressure they’re applying.
Some have been covered by his medical insurance, which allows for replacements around every five years, he says.
He bought his third prosthetic hand, for example, from eBay.
“It’s funny to think I bought a secondhand second hand,” he says.
The phenomenon “makes no sense physiologically,” says Chris Duncan, a rehabilitation doctor and chief medical officer at BIOS, a neurotechnology company that is supporting the trial.
Stretching a typical hand pulls on tendons that extend down the forearm.
There aren’t any tendons in a bionic arm—Davidson’s “stretches” are just moving actuators, says Duncan.
“What Avi’s experiencing is kind of like uncharted territory, honestly,” he says.

The accident resulted in second- and third-degree burns over 37% of his body, says Davidson, “and I broke my back in approximately 50 separate locations.” He also broke eight ribs, and his spinal cord was severed.
He’s pretty sure he broke his left wrist, too.
But around 10 days later, his left hand—his dominant hand, and the one he’d grabbed the wire with—had started to develop gangrene.
The team also inserted 24 electrodes into the muscles around the nerves.
Wires for each of the nerve arrays and for pairs of muscle electrodes were left protruding from Davidson’s skin.
After the surgery, he was offered some time to recover.
“By day two, I’m like ‘No, let’s get me on the machines,’” he says.
Davidson has been using the hand at home since July 10, and he has noticed improvements.
At first it took him a few minutes to write his name; now he can manage it in seconds.
“They need to understand that this is a useful new technological paradigm that will bring value to patients,” says Duncan.
Team members also hope the technology will allow users to operate other devices, such as remote controls and wheelchairs.
The surgeon exposed three nerves in Davidson’s arm and implanted an electrode array containing 100 needles in each one.
To get it up and running, the team had to train the device in two directions.
The first involved converting nerve activity into hand, wrist, and finger movements.
That part was easy, says George: “It takes a matter of about five minutes.”
The second direction—linking the electrodes to sensations felt by the prosthetic—is much more time-consuming.
They’d then turn up the signal at each of those points to see the effect.
“It’s like a three-day process,” says George.
The hand can be useful, but it has also proved surprising.
This could be what’s known as “phantom pain”—a symptom experienced by some people who have lost a limb.

Some have been covered by his medical insurance, which allows for replacements around every five years, he says. Others he’s had to buy himself. He bought his third prosthetic hand, for example, from eBay. “It’s funny to think I bought a secondhand second hand,” he says. Davidson turned out to be an ideal candidate, says Jake George, director of the university’s neurorobotics lab . Davidson, who was keen to take part, first had to undergo what George describes as “pretty extensive” physical and psychological evaluations. Not only did he have to be well enough for surgery, but the team also scanned his brain to make sure that he still had a mental representation of his left hand—suggesting he’d be able to move a bionic one. They also ran tests to check that the nerves in his arm were working. That part was easy, says George: “It takes a matter of about five minutes.” The second direction—linking the electrodes to sensations felt by the prosthetic—is much more time-consuming. They’d then turn up the signal at each of those points to see the effect. “It’s like a three-day process,” says George. They focused on Davidson’s personal goals—he wanted to be able to cook at home, so the pair worked on strategies to hold and manipulate utensils, prepare and chop ingredients, and carry plates and bowls. “He was able to crack an egg,” says Seckinger. “He made an omelet.” Davidson has been using the hand at home since July 10, and he has noticed improvements. At first it took him a few minutes to write his name; now he can manage it in seconds. “The things I’m able to do with it now are tremendous, comparatively to where I was at initially,” he says. The hand can be useful, but it has also proved surprising. Sometimes, Davidson feels pain in it. This could be what’s known as “phantom pain”—a symptom experienced by some people who have lost a limb. Curiously, he also says he experiences wrist strain. Davidson says he’s been getting a stiffness in his prosthetic wrist similar to what he experiences when he’s been typing for a long time with his flesh-and-blood right hand. He’s also realized that he can relieve the tension by pulling the bionic fingers back to stretch out his prosthetic wrist. “It’s weird,” he says. Davidson will have his implants and the hand for a couple more months at least. But the trial was designed to run for “at least” one year, and that year will be up by the end of January 2027. “I’m not quite sure what happens after that,” he says. George hopes the trial could be extended, but that will depend on funding. “From our perspective, we’d like to go as long as we can,” he says. “We don’t want to leave Avi without support.” Davidson isn’t too worried about what comes next, though. “I went into this knowing that this was not something that I get to keep,” he says. “I am not going to benefit from this … I wanted to be a part of this in the context of being able to help push the technology forward.” Scientists hope it could be used to reconstruct a person’s inner thoughts, mental images, or even dreams. story.title: The next generation of bionic hands is here—and they can feel

facts.text: Davidson, now 33 and a trauma therapist, went on to have physical therapy and adjusted to life in his changed body.
The first one, which he received a year and a half after his injury, was a basic hook that allowed him to pick things up.
It wasn’t fancy, but it gave him “a psychological feeling of returning to being whole,” he says.
The hand is part of the bionic LUKE arm, named after Luke Skywalker of Star Wars , who was fitted with a lifelike prosthetic arm after his own was light-sabered off .
The arm was developed in the 2000s , initially trialed in 2014 , and approved by the FDA that same year.
The trial that Davidson is enrolled in isn’t so focused on the arm itself but on a new way to connect it to a person’s nervous system.
The connection allows users to control movements and receive feedback about how much pressure they’re applying.
Some have been covered by his medical insurance, which allows for replacements around every five years, he says.
He bought his third prosthetic hand, for example, from eBay.
“It’s funny to think I bought a secondhand second hand,” he says.
The phenomenon “makes no sense physiologically,” says Chris Duncan, a rehabilitation doctor and chief medical officer at BIOS, a neurotechnology company that is supporting the trial.
Stretching a typical hand pulls on tendons that extend down the forearm.
There aren’t any tendons in a bionic arm—Davidson’s “stretches” are just moving actuators, says Duncan.
“What Avi’s experiencing is kind of like uncharted territory, honestly,” he says.

The accident resulted in second- and third-degree burns over 37% of his body, says Davidson, “and I broke my back in approximately 50 separate locations.” He also broke eight ribs, and his spinal cord was severed.
He’s pretty sure he broke his left wrist, too.
But around 10 days later, his left hand—his dominant hand, and the one he’d grabbed the wire with—had started to develop gangrene.
The team also inserted 24 electrodes into the muscles around the nerves.
Wires for each of the nerve arrays and for pairs of muscle electrodes were left protruding from Davidson’s skin.
After the surgery, he was offered some time to recover.
“By day two, I’m like ‘No, let’s get me on the machines,’” he says.
Davidson has been using the hand at home since July 10, and he has noticed improvements.
At first it took him a few minutes to write his name; now he can manage it in seconds.
“They need to understand that this is a useful new technological paradigm that will bring value to patients,” says Duncan.
Team members also hope the technology will allow users to operate other devices, such as remote controls and wheelchairs.
The surgeon exposed three nerves in Davidson’s arm and implanted an electrode array containing 100 needles in each one.
To get it up and running, the team had to train the device in two directions.
The first involved converting nerve activity into hand, wrist, and finger movements.
That part was easy, says George: “It takes a matter of about five minutes.”
The second direction—linking the electrodes to sensations felt by the prosthetic—is much more time-consuming.
They’d then turn up the signal at each of those points to see the effect.
“It’s like a three-day process,” says George.
The hand can be useful, but it has also proved surprising.
This could be what’s known as “phantom pain”—a symptom experienced by some people who have lost a limb.
